OFFICER.—DEFEa't OF _REBELS. MANDALAY, FEBRUARY 16 —A deputation of twenty-two principal Chinese traders in Mandalay waited to-day on Mr. Bernard to complain of the proceedings of Captain Burrows, Assistant Provost Marshal. They stated that on the'l3th, accompanied by some Sepays, he forcibly broke into the house of a leading Chinese merchant, and his subordinates seized there a lot of valuable property, and that he arrested without canes several Chinese merchants. The petitioners declare that unless protection is afforded to them it will be impossible for the Chinese to reside or carry on business in Mandalay. CALCUTTA, SUNDAY.—Disturbances are reported in the southern portion of the Bassein district. A large body of armed men met and were routed by a force of police, but the whole country being a network of creeks it is difficult to follow the fugitives and crush the rising. Sepoys were promptly despatched to the spot, and her Majesty's ship Ranger has gene to Bassein. The Shwegyin rising seems to be finally suppressed. The main body of rebels, while retreating, were met by the Salween police and completely routed. Two Phoomeyee leaders were killed, over a hundred prisoners were taken, and much booty was recovered. We have received a copy of the following despatch from the Viceroy, dated Rangoon, Monday :—" I regret to re- port that St. Barbet deputy commissioner at Bassein, was killed yesterday. He had broken up a party of dacoits, and had driven them into an island, which he surrounded with police and launches. Unfortunately he landed with only a single peon. I deeply regret his loss, as he was an officer of great ability." SPEECH BY LORD DUFFERIN. MANDALAY, VIA TEHERAN', FEBRUARY 18TH.—All is quiet at Bhamo, and trade is reviving. The expedition to the Shin States will start early next month and Inlayywa, 130 miles from Mandalay, will be the headquarters of the expedition, for this season. The, Viceroy walked through Mandalay Bazaar on the 18th inst. Lady Dufferin's recep- tion on the previous day was attended by the leading Ma- homedan ladies, as well as by the Burmese ladies. They all went away delighted with the reception. At a dinner given at the Palace on the evening of the 18th, the Viceroy, after some observations in praise of General Prendergast s military operations, and after announcing that a gratuity of 300,000 rupees was granted to the Burmese expeditionary force, said :—The invasion of Burma k was undertaken with regret by the Indian Government. We had no quarrel with the inhabitants of the country, and the conquest of the country, whatever might be the ultimate advantages, was certain to be fraught with immediate anxiety and embarrass- ments. On the other hand, the existing relations between ourselves and the Burmese Court had become intolerable, inasmuch as they were fast tending to jeopardise the secu- rity and most vital interests of our territories. We therefore I chose the lesser of two evils, determined to put an end to the I rule of a prince who was a curse to his own subjects and an impossible neighbour: THE EASTERN CRISIS.—PROSPECT OF PEACE. CONSTANTINOPLE, SATURDAY.—It is rumoured that an alliance has hen definitely arranged between Servia and Greece under the auspices of Austria and France. The Porte continues to regard the attitude of Greece with great anxiety. BUCHAREST, MONDA.Y. The peace negotiations enter to-day into an entirely new phase. They were began doubt- less with equal goodwill by the delegates on either side. The Servian delegates especially desired to conclude a treaty, not only of peace, but also of friendship, and by the instrument of peace itself to eradicate the cause of seven years' misunderstanding. The Bulgarian delegate's attitude was, however, discouraging. Thus the first sittings revealed a somewhat haggling tendency, and M. Mijatoyics there- fore demanded that the whole Bulgarian treaty should be presented to the Conference. The Bulgarian delegate de- clined doing so unless the Servian projct were simulta- neously presented. BELGRADE, MONDAY.-11 Royal decree was issued here yesterday, ordering the immediate withdrawel to Nisch of the Servian troops near Pirot.

VIENNA, MONDAY.—The latest advices received here irorn Athens encourage the hope that Greece will renounce the warlike projects now that she saes no support from Eng- land is to be looked for in carrying them out. letter from a British naval officer at Sada Bay states that the English squadron is surrounded by Turkish, Italian, and Austrian men-of-war, but the Turkish vessels are of such a character that the Greeks would make short work of them in a fight. THE SOUDAN.—THE " GORDON " PAPER MONEY. CAIRO, SUNDAY.—Diecovery has been made at the Ministry of Finance of a strong " ring " for the issue of fic- titious " Gordon " bonds. Had the scheme been success- fully carried out it would have entailed a loss upon the Government of about t 20,000. Several Government officiate and financiers are compromised in the affair, which is now being investigated. EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN. CAIRO, WEDNESDAY.—A conference was held yesterday between Sir Henry Wolff, Lieutenant-Generat Sir Frederick Stephenson, Sir Evelyn Baring, and Major-General Grenfell, at which the question of the settlement of the frontier and the re-occupation of Dongola was discussed. Opinions, pronouncing for and against the re-occupation, have been drafted and sent to the authorities in London. The military authorities here, as well as the natives, are in favour of the measure. PRINCE BISMARCK AND THE POLES. BERLIN, MONDAY.—The debate on the first reading of the bills for strengthening the German element in the eastern provinces of Prussia came on to-day in the Lower House of the Prussian Diet. It was opened by the Polish deputy Herr von Wierzbinski who protested in passionate terms against the first or the measures, which provides for the establishment of German settlers, and declared that Poland would not perish in the life and death struggle thus forced upon her. Dr. Lucius, Minister of Agriculture, declared in reply that the bill was an act of necessity and self-defence, as the Poles were unwilling to consider themselves Prussian subjects, and always cherished the hope of a Polish restora- tion, notwithstanding that it was the Prussian kings alone who raised Posen from her prostrate condition and intro- duced agrarian'and social prosperity. The object of the bill was to secure a settled and capable peasantry and working- ' class—in fact to establish whole colonies in the Polish pro- vinces. CF THE PROPOSED EXH`BITION. PARIS, SATURDAY.—The Government has decided to maintain the international character of the proposed Na- tional Isahibition to be held at Paris in 1889, and it will consequently be open to all nations. GERMAN ANNEXATIONS IN THE PACIFIC. BERLIN, MONDAY.—The German Ambassador in London has officially notified to the British Foreign Office that the Marshall, Brown, and Providence Islands in the Pacific, have been placed trader the proteetion of Germany. FRANCE AND MADAGASCAR. TAISTATIVE, FEBRUARY 14Tre—Admiral Mint has arrived here from Antananarivo with the ratification of the treaty of peace concluded between France and Madagascar. INTERNATIONAL LEGISLATION. PARIS, THURSDAY.—It is stated that the French Socialist Deputies have sent an address to the English working-men members of Parliament proposing to organise a movement for international legislation in the matter of labour, and holding a great European Congress on the question. THE NEW SOUTH WALES MINISTRY. SYDNEY, THURSDAY.— Sir Patrick Jennings and Sir John Robertson have formed a coalition Ministry inclnding the leading man of both parties. THE INSULT TO THE QUEEN OF SPAIN. MADRID, THURSDAY.—The Supreme Council of War is stated to have confirmed the court-martial's sentence of eight you's' imprisonment and loss of rank upon Lieut.-Col. Don Enrique de Borbon for misconduct in December last, while on duty at the Palace. aw.•••••• 1

James Bateman, vicar of Haile, was summoned for assaulting Nancy Blanchard, his house- keeper.—The magistrates considered that Bateman had as- saulted the complainant, but, as she had forgiven him on receiving a sovereign, they dismissed the case. CONVERSATIONAL SEALING WAX.—Frivolons people in fashionable circles who have become tired of the Language of Flowers have adopted what they call a new code of col- our, sealing-wax being the instrument of their am u sement Red wax most only be used to seal business let ters, and black is of course reserved for mourning correspondence. Blue is significant of love, and five tints of various blueness are now manufactured, so that each stage of the tender passion may have its corresponding coloured 'wax. Pink wax is to he kept exclusively for sealing lett3rs of congrat- ulation, and white is to be employed for wedding and hall invitations. Variegated or mottled wax is to express con- flicting ecaotions on the part of those who use it. Sax C. DenßE's DEFENCE.—A resolution was recently passed by the council of the Chelsea Liberal and Ridical ' Association exonerating" Sir C. Dilke. The proceedings were private; . hut, according to a published report, Sir Charles adverted to the recent 14il proceedings with which he has been connected. With regard to the question which bad been raised by some people as to the reason why he did not enter the witness box and challenge the evidence brought to bear against him, Sir Charles said that be acted entirely upon the advice of his counsel in this matter. So far as be was concerned he was fully prepared, and had ex- nected up to the last, to have appeared in the witness box. There was a division of opinion among his friends as to •whether it was advisable for him to take that course, and he therefore had decided, as his legal advisers were not of one mind with regard to this point, to enter the box. How- ever, at the eleventh hour, they unanimously agreed that it was quite an unneceesary act of procedure, and he therefore gave way. This was this the only reason which had induc- ed him to rel,rain from giving personal .evidence.—It is stated that Sir C. Dilke's solicitor has offered to place all his information in the hands of the Queen's Proctor, in case that official decides to intervene in the Crawford suit. IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter past four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Earl of Oetsnow moved for a re- turn relating to agricultural holdings in England and Wales.—Earl S.PENCER promised that immediately after the agricultu-al returns for this year were published, supple- mentary returns should be printed, giving as far as possible the information which the noble earl desired.--The sub- ject of the war with hurrnah was afterwards brought before their lordships, the Earl of KIMBERLEY moving that the consent of the House be given to the application of the irevenues of India to defray the expenses of the military operations undertaken by the late Government, which he I held were justifiable.--Lord Harris, the Duke of Cambridge, Earl Northbrook, Lord Cranbrook, the Earl of Kimberley, land the Marquis of Salisbury took part in the debate, the latter expressing an opinion that the war will turn out, lafter two or three years, for the advantage not less of the Indian Empire than of the people whom we have subjected. —The motion was agreed to.—Lord CRANBROOK then in- quired whether the elovernment would lay upon the table such information as could be given without injury to the public service on the present condition of Ireland in respect to boycotting and similar outrages.—Earl SPENCER com- plained that notice had not been given of the question.—The return was agreed to, and their lordships adjourned at ten minutes past seven. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QUESTIONS, 4.k.c —The report of the Committee appointed to inquire into the recent riots in London was laid upon the table of the House of Commons by Mr. Childers. The re- port concludes with a strong opinion that the administration and organi.ation of the Metropolitan Police Force requires to be thoroughly investigated, and suggests that such in- vestigation should take place without delay. The right hon. gentleman stated that be had communicated the substance of the report to the Chief Com- missioner of Police (Sir E. Henderson), who had forwarded a letter placing his resignation in his hands. The resignation had been accepted, and no time would be lost in instituting an inquiry with a view to re- medying the defects in the force which had been pointed out. He would on Thursday state what would be the char- acter of the proposed inquiry.—Mr. CHLIVREELAIN informed Lord Curzon that the Government intended to introduce a bill dealing with county government at the earliest possible moment, and it would contain the proposals of the Govern- ment with regard to the reform of local taxatien.—Referr- ing to the charges against the Provost Marshal at Mandalay, Sir U. KAY-SITITTTLEWORTII stated that the investigation showed that Colonel Hooper did photograph men under- going execution, but the prisoners were blindfolded and did net know they were being photographed, nor were the exe- cutions in any way protracted. On one occasion an attempt was made, under the Provost Marshal's orders, to extract evidence by the threat of execution. For both these offences the Provost Marshal would be severely censured and refused the preferment which he had otherwise deserved.—The Premier was asked if it was the intention of the Govern- ment to suppress the National Leagae —Mr. GLADSTONE stated in reply that the Government were anxious to see the authority of the Crown in Ireland restored to that full state of efficiency which it enjoyed in England and Scotland, but they were led to think that it would not be wise, or justifiable, or politic on their part to seek the restoration of order through the medium of an immediate application to Parliament for special criminal legislation. PARLIAMENTARY PROCEDURE.—Mr. GLADSTONE then moved that the notices of motion relating to Parliamentary procedure and the East India, Burmah (Expenses of Mili- tary Operations) hawe precedence of the orders of the day. —Sir M. HICKS-BEACII thought the motion if passed would establish a very inconvenient precedent, and suggested that the order for Supply should be postponed.—Mr. GLADSTONE replied that the Government thought the subject of such importance that there ought not to be material delay in dealing with it.—The motion was then agreed to, and Mr. GLADSTONE moved that a Select Committee be appointed to consider the question of procedure in the House of Com- mons and to re.port as to the amendment of existing rules and upon any new rules which they may consider desirable for the efficient despatch of business. In proposing the Committee the Government charged themselves with the responsibility of making known at once and in full to the Committee the views which the Government entertained on all points of the greatest importance, and that was the course the Government would take. He was glad to find that they appeared to be united in the opinion that it was not by penal and restrictive measures but by a judicious use of the means of multiplying their mode of action that they might hope for the greatest and most effective progress.--Sir M. HICKS-BEACH hoped it would be remembered that the Conservative party were as anxious to make the House of Commons, of which they were all proud, as efficient for Its work as was any Liberal or Radical. He hoped the la- bours of the Committee might have a successful issue.— Lord HARTINGTON expressed his satisfaction with the course taken by the Government, and said he was entirely in favour of remedial rather than coercive or restrictive legislation, but he thought the question of the closure ought not to be excluded from the consideration of the committee. The motion was then agreed to. THE BITEMAH EXPEDITION.—Sir U. KAY-SHIITTLEIVOIITH moved that the cost of the expedition to Burmah be charged on the revenues of India, and after making a statement similar to that made by Lord Kimbet ley in the House of Peers, he appealed to his friends outside the House, more especially those connected with the country he represented, net to form exaggerated anticipations of any benefits that might accrue from the annexation.—air. HUNTER moved as an amendment that it would be unjust to defray the ex- penses of the military operations out of the revenues of India. He asserted that the annexation was universally condemned by the Indian press, and that the people who had clamoured for it were the Chambers of Commerce in this country echoing the sentiments of the English merchants at Rangoon.—The motion was seconded by Mr. H. RICHARD.— The House divided. For the resolution, 297; for the amendment, 82; majority for the resolution, 215. The House adjourned at twenty-five minutes to two o'clock.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TIJESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TIJESDAY.

The Lord -Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. VOLITNTEERS AND COAST DEFENCES.—Lord SIDMOUTII asked if the First Lord of the Admiralty would lay on the table the reports of Admiral Hamilton on coast defences, and on the Royal Naval Volunteer Artillery Corps, with re- ports from any other officer commissioned te inquire into either or both of these matter6.—The Marquis ocitirox ad- mitted the importance of the subject. Admiral Hamilton had prepared a teport, and the inqniry was continued by Sir Robert Molineux9 but had tot been completed. THE LONDON RlOT.—Lord ENFIELD inquired whether in the year 1879 a Departmental Committee was appointed by the then Secretary of State for the Home Department to inquire into and report as to the constitution and condition of the Metropolitan Police Force, and if such a report was , made whether there would be any objection to present it to Parliament?—Lord TIICRLOW said the report of the com- mittee of 1879 partook largely of the character of a confi- dential document, and it would not be possible for the Home Office to lay the whole of it upon the table. The House rose at 5-10. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QUESTIONS.-Sir L. PLAYFAIR stated that the Govern. ;nem did not intend to deal with the important question of free education until they knew the results of the labours of
SATURDAY
'JR,
F

J the Royal Commission which had Nen issued on the sub- ject of elementary education generally.—Mr. BRYCE infor- med Mr. B. Coleridge that the Government were not of opinion that the present would be a favourable moment to approach the Sultan with a view to obtaining hem him a concession of territory to Greece.—Furtber information was given by Sir U. Kay-Shuttlaworth relative to the conduct of the Provost Marshal with the expedition to Upper Bur- mah. . THE TAXATION OF IRELAND.—Sir J. IWKENNA called at- tention to the inequality of Imperial taxation, in Ireland, and moved for certain returns'—Slr T. EsafoNna seconded the motion.—Mr. GOSCHEN thought the returns would not show whether Ireland was paying too much or too little. What was wanted was that principles should be grappled with by a Committee of the House, and that then, applying those principles, they should see if they could come to some , agreement.—Sir J. LUBBOCK was of opinion that the House needed more reliable facts on which to base the taxation of , Ireland.—Mr. JOHN DILLoN congratulated the House on having listened to the first speech Mr. Goschen had made in favour of Ireland, and said the reason for the change would no doubt grow stronger every day.—Mr. H. FOWLER promised to give the returns ask-d for, and pointed oat that the extra burden of taxation imposed during the last twenty years had been borne to a great extent by Great Britain and not by Ireland.—Mr. GLADSTONE argued that there were other relations between England and Ireland besides those of direct taxation which ought to be taken in view, and said he was sure the Irish members would admit, that Ire- land had received advantages from theme of Imperial credit. It might be that there might, he said, be further and mere extended attempts to settle questions affecting Ireland, such as the land question brought up which would make it necessary that the House and the Government should come to a conclusive and solid judgment of the pro- pertions of the relative taxes paid.—After some discussion, the motion amended so as to include returns relating to Scot- land and England was agreed to. ROYALTIES.—Leave was given to Mr. Warmington to bring in a bill to render owners of mining royalties and dues liable to local rates, and to amend the Rating Act,

1874. EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY. MI. O'CONNOR moved the second reading of the Employers' Liability Act (1880) Amendment Bill. He explained that the bill proposed to render null and void all contracts in which workmen under- took not to receive the benefit of the Act.—After considera- ble discussion, the bill was read a second time and referred to a Select Committee, with power to inquire into the oper- ation of the Act of 1880. The House adjourned at 12-40. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at ten minutes past 12 o'clock. HOUSE TENURE IN IRELAND.—Mr. D. CateLy moved the second reading of Tenure of the Towns Houses (Ireland) Bill. Fe said the demand for a reform of the law as to houses in tewns was not exclusively an Irish grievance. He only asked the House to 'affirm the principles that tenants of houses in towns should, like tenants in agricultural holdings, be entitled to compensation for the improvements they made.—,Mr. J. MORLEY said it could scarcely be des- cribed as a simple, small, and practical matter. It involved an appeal to very important principles, and contained a great many intricate details. He did not think that the bad state of property in towns in Ireland was entirely due to the law of tenure. Houses were not like land, because land was fixed by nature, lent house accommodation was simply a matter of supply and demand. In one er two details he consi- dered that the scheme of the bill was not well conceived.— Mr. SEXTON hoped the right hon. gentleman would be able to announce on an early day that the Government would take up the measure—Mr. E. R. RUSSELL said the hope of many of the supporters of the bill was that by inserting the thin end of the wedge they should be able to extend from agriculture the principle they believed to be sound and just to urban property, and also to extend from Ireland the same principle to the general property of Great Britain.—Mr. GOSCHEN asked whet„Per it would be wise to undertake legis- lation that would create a double ownership in house pro- perty.—Mr. GLADSTONE repeated the reason why it was not possible for the Government to accept the second read- ing of the bill. The Government answer to the bill was that the hardship, so far from being exceptional and peculiar to Ireland, was felt to a much greater extent in England and Scotland.—Mr. Came, expressed satisfaction with the Prime Minister's statement and withdrew the bill.

COPYHOLDS.—Mr. C. H. JAMES moved the second read- ing of the Copyhold Enfranchisement Bill, which was passed last session by the Commons but was rejected by the Lords. The hon. member referred to the copvholds of the Raw- tenstall and Clitheroe districts, and dwelt on the necessity of getting rid of them, Tbe bill was read a second time.— On the motion of the second reading of the Metropolitan Water Supply Bill, Mr. BROADHURST stated that the Government could not accept it because they would shortly be considering a scheme for the better government of Lon- don.—The dek,ate was proceeding when the time for ad- journment arrived. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIIIRSDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—A bill, the object of which is to re- move eels from the operation of the Freshwater Fisheries Act, was read a second time.—Lord THURLOW, speaking for the Home Office, stated that it was not the intention of the Government to declare illegal all public meetings and pro- cessions in the squares and parks on Sundays, and advised that discussion on the subject should be suspended pending the decision as to the steps to be taken with a view, if pos- sible, to improve the existing arrangements which governed such proceedings.—A brief discussion on the operations of the National League in Ireland followed. Their Lordships adjourned at five minntes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMNONS.—THIIRSDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QUESTIONS, &C.—Mr. CHILDERS announced that he pro- posed to introduce a bill giving to tradesmen who suffered loss owing to the riots in the Metropolis such compensation as appeared to be just out of the Metropolitan Police Fund. The right hon. gentleman assured Mr. Picton that as the action of the Convocation of Canterbury in summoning a House of Laymen did not violate the Act of Henry VIII. it old not entail any punishment.—Mr. BRADLAUGH elicited the information that Sir H. D. Wolff will receive a salary during his mission, that the cost of telegrams sent out to him was £772. and that the cost of those received from him was £3,192.—Mr. CHILDERS told Mr. Newhes that as Lord Randolph Churchill's recent speech was de- livered out of England it was no part of his duty to consider the speech with a view to institute a prosecution.—Upon this Mr. SEXTON gave notice that he would move a resolu- tion condemning the language used, and Lord R. CHURCH- ILL intimated that when the notice appeared upon the paper he should ask the Prime Minister to appoint a day for its discussion. Referring to the distress in Ire- land, Mr. J. MORLEY stated that the situation was a serious one. It was being carefelly watched, anil the Go- vernment would not hesitate to apply for further powers if occasion arose. The right hon. gentleman explained that under existing powers outdoor relief could not be afforded to able-bodied men while there was room in the workhouse. —Mr. CHILDERS stated that the inquiry into the organisa- tion of the Metropolitan police would be,conducted by a departmental committee over which he himself would pre- side. SUPPLY.—The House then went into Committee of Supply on the remaining Supplementary Civil Service Estimates. Upon progress being reported, Mr. TREVELYAN introduced the Crofters' Bill.

Kay, Brothe,..s, titockport.—Adet, MURDER ON THE HIGH SEAS.—At Southampton, on Monday, James Whelan, was remanded on the charge of murdering George Richardson on the high seas on Nov. 15th. The deceased was the mate of the brigantine Emma Shaw, the prisoner being a seaman on board. A dispute arose between them, and prisoner swore that he would kill the mate. The next night Whelan struck the mate on the head with an iron belaying-pin, and then pushed him over- board, and he was not seen again. A SINGULAR DISCOvEnv. A few days since the Old Berkeley Foxhounds, when hunting in the woody district ci Taplow, ran a fine fox to earth, and it was determined to dig out the animal. On this being done the remains of five dead foxhounds were discovered in the lair, which without doubt are the bones of the five foxhounds belonging to this pack which on the same day exactly IS years ago were lost at this spot, and of which, despite all efforts made at the time to recover them, no trace until the present had ever been found. It is almost certain that these dogs, having followed the fbx to earth, were afterwards unabll to find an exit, and thus perished. W. D. THE STATE OF IRELAND. William Galvin, a bailiff on an estate near Ballinasloe, who had been concerned in some ejectment proceedings, was a few weeks ago upbraided for his conduct by a couple of men and then terribly assaulted, and his injuries tern:tin. ated fatally on Monday night. MOONLIGHTERS AGLIN. - Several tenants on Lord Ormathvvaite's property, near Listowel, have been visited by moonlighters. The men were armed and disguised. After firing the shots they made the tenants swear that they would pay no rent unless they received a reduction of 50 per cent LOYALIST DEMONSTRATION.—A. monster Loyalist demu- stration took place on Saturday in Stewardstown, county Tyrone, against any Rome Rule scheme being granted. The meeting was composed of Liberals and Conservatives. Resolutioms were passed opposing any scheme, and pledging those present to maintain the Union.

SUPPOSED MURDER IN IRELAND.—The police at Car- rickmore, Tyrone, have received information that the body of a woman had been found lying on the mountain at Crag- aconry, near Pomeroy. The officers who proceeded to the spot found a woman, about thirty years of age, with a mark on the left eyebrow and blood on the nostrils. Her hands were clenched and bloodstained, bearing evidences of a straggle. She was recognised as a Mrs 111`Annally, of Toombridge, but the cause of death is a mystery. MR. Devere ON Otrretactas.—Mr. Davitt, addressing a meeting in County Kerry on Sandie-. made an earnest ap- peal to the people from committing outrages. He said he did not know among the scum of unadorned scoundreliern in human nature a creature so vile and contemptible as the man who would carry out the purpose of the burglar and the cutpurse under the guise of patriotism. He begged them, for the sake of their county and for the sake of victory, to stop these senseless criminal proceedings, and to cease tp play into their enemies' hands. UNBIDDEN GUESTS.—An extraordinary affray occurred near Castleisland, county Kerry, on Saturday night. A disguised party of young men entered a farmhouse where a wedding was being celebrated, as guests, this, it is said, be- ing a custom of the country. but a party of police rushed in after them to arrest them as moonlighters. A fight en- sued. The police, repulsed, sent for reinforcements. The battle was renewed, and the police, again repulsed, summoned more reinforcements. This time 40 men came, and arrested 19 of the wedding party and the unbidden guests. CHARGE OF ARSON AGAINST A J.P.—At Timoleague (county Cork) Petty Sessions, on Monday, Mr. John A. Lucas, J.P., and his wife were charged with attempted arson on January 19. Mr. Lucas's residence at Clonakilty was under the protection of two policemen, owing to out- rages committed there. On the night in question the police went to inspect the out offices, and on their return found the parlone on fire, the curtains and floor being saturated ! with paraffin oil, Mrs. Moore, who came down dressed after a very short time, suggested that the fire was caused from without, but this was impossible, the place being barricaded. The case was adjourned. THE IRISH CATHOLIC BISHOPS' REPLY TO MR. GLAD- STONE.—A letter has been addressed to the Prime Minis- ter by the Archbishop of Dublin acting on behalf of the Catholic Bishops of Ireland. Dr. Walsh says it is the firm and conscientious conviction of the rrish prelates that self- government or Home Rule alone can satisfy the wants, the wishes. and the legitimate aspirations of the people. and they are satisfied that the demand for Home Rule put for- ward in the result of the recent elections in no way transgresses the conatitutional limits marked out by Mr. Gladstone. The land question calls for a final solution, and this, they believe, cannot better be effected than by the purchase by the Government of the landed interest in the noil, and the reletting of the land to tenant farmers at a flaw° very considerably below the present judicial rents. They are of opinion that no just cause of complaint in re- gard to :he question of " social order " will or can exist i after the settlement of the land question on such a basis. The Premier has tendered to the ArcWshop his " sincere thanks for this communication." ARRIVAL OF THE NEW VICEROY.—On Saturday morning, the Earl and Countess of Aberdeen, arrived at Kingston in the speCial mail steamer Ulster, which was moored alongside Carlisle Pier. The guardship fired a Royal salute of 21 guns. During Lord Aberdeen's State entry into Dublin in the afternoon some disturbmces occurred in College Green, opposite Trinity College. The students had assembled in a body at the gates, and cheered for the Queen, and a large mob, which filled the space before the Bank of Ireland (the old House of Commons), responded with loud cheers for Parnell. The students cheered for Lord Rindolph Churchill and the Prince of Wales. The mole replied with cheers for Home Rule, Mr. Morley, and an Irish Parliament. Subse- quently the students began throwing money amongst the crowd, and in the rush which ensned a number of people were injured. The Earl and Countess of Aberdeen received the first address of welcome in Dublin, on Monday, from the Kingstown Commissioners. The Viceroy, replying, said : Your expressions of welcome and goodwill towards Lady Aberdeen and myself are warmly appreciated by us. Most sincerely do I join with you in those hopes and aspirations with which your address concludes. It is my earnest hope and purpose that during my tenure of the high office to which I have been appointed me action may he invariably in accordance with all that is for the best interest of the country. I concur with the views expressed as to the great value of technical education both socially and commercially, audit will be may aim to enlarge the facilities at present existing in this respect. His Excellency added that it would not be appropriate for him to enter into a discussion of the political topics in the address, but he should make her Majesty's Government aware of the views which they bad set forth. The Lord Mayor of Dublin Mr. Harrington. M.P., E. D. Gray, Mr. Murphy, and Mr. Peter MacDonald, members of Parliament and ex o.,fficio members of the Coun- cil of the Chamber of Commerce, have forwarded to the Lord-Lieutenant a statement dissenting from certain views in the address presented by the Council to hie Excellency. This statement asserts that with English rule in its pre- sent form the Irish people would never be content, and against it they would never cease to struggle. They de- sire the control of their own affairs, leaving the empire un- broken and all Imperial affairs in the hands of the Imperial Parliament. LORD R. CHURCHILL IN IRELAND. Lord Randolph Churchill arrived in Ulster on Monday and had an enthusias- tic reception. In acknowledging some Orauge and Conser- vative addresses at Larne his lordship contrasted the state of Ireland now with its condition at the time his father was Lord Lieutenant, and said that at the earlier period nobody would have supposed that a British Minister would now have been contemplating a policy which must inevitably, if carried to a successful issue, not only dissolve the connec- tion between Ireland and Great Britain, but must, he firmly believed, shatter the British Empire. This attack was headed by an experienced statesman who was animated by little principle at all, except the great principle of main- taining himself in power at any cost. It was utterly im- possible that the loyal and prosperous North of Ireland could ever be placed under the domination of a Dublin Par- liament, and he could assure them that in this struggle they might.coant on the assistance and sapport of all the members of the late Government and the whole Tory party in England. Addressing a crowd at the Larne railway station, Lord Randolph said the privileges enjoyed by the people of the North of Ireland as compared with other parts of Ireland were worth defending and worth demonstrating for. It might be that they were worth fighting for, though he did not expect it would come to this. In the evening his lordship addressed a great meeting in the Ulster Hall, Belfast. He said there could be no doubt that the polity of the Government was a policy which involved the repeal of the legislative union. The Tory party in England were de- termined to offer to such a policy the most strenuous resis- tance, and no doubt in that resistance they would have the sympathy of many persons of position in the Liberal ranks- but it was essential for them to know to what extent this resolution would receive support in Ireland, a point on which a good deal of uncertainty existed in public opinion in England. Lord Randolph Churchill left Belfast on Tuesday afternoon, on his journey back to London. He previously drove to the Ulster Club. and lunched there with the local leaders of the Orange and Conservative parties.

Contingents came from every Part of London. and speeches were delivered from, three waggonettes in the neighbourhood of the Reformers Tree. Notwithstanding that many taousands of persons had assembled the proceedings were orderly throughout. The police, mounted and unmounted, were present in large numbers. TWENTY-FOUR RACEHORSES BURNT TO DEATH. The well-known American stable of the Meadow Brook Club has been totally destroyed by fire. The fire broke out at t,Vo o'clock on the Morning of the 100 inst. The animals belonged to various owners, raanv of whom are amateur riders of ability. The four stabien;en who slept on the pre- mises were wakened by the crying and kicking of the horses, and when aroused the fire had a firm hold of the structftre, which was burned to the ground. There were 25 horses in the stable, and out of these only °IA was saved, viz., Mr. Elliot Roosevelt's hunter, Mohawk, which was in the most northern stall. Amongst the animals whichlwere burnt were many of note and of great promise. " MIN NIG-REY."— " ERNE...ST LIN V4'oo D." —" 4.1. div.p: - GENERAL NEWS.

' On Sunday morning the publishing premises of the _Northern Daily Mail at West Hartlepool were completely destroyed by fire. Edwin Burt Pearse, a Salvationist, was committed for trial at Warminster, on Monday, fer the wilful murder ,of his wife, who was found dead in bed, having been poisoned. His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales arrived at Paris on Monday morning, and proceeded to the Hotel Bristol. The Prince of Wales continued his journey to Cannes on Tuesday evening. The Council of the Liberation Society on Tuesday passed a resolution expressing satisfaction that an unprecedeeted number of members favourable to religious equality were returned at the general election. The Duke of Marlborough seems determined to get rid of a great portion of his ancestral possessions. It is said that the whole of the pictures at Blenheim, except the family portraits, will be brought to the hammer. CARDINAL NEWMAN'S BIRTHDAY.—Cardinal Newman completed his 85th year on Saturday. Considering his great age he is in remarkably good health. He received many congratulations from all parts of the country. NEW Inisn BISHOP.—Tbe Pope has confirmed the election ' of the Vicar Capitular, the Rev. Patrick McAllister, Parish Priest of Ballycastle, co. Antrim, to the Bishopric of Down and Connor, vacant by the death of Bishop Dorrier. The hearing of the Stepney election petition was resumed on Tuesday, and in the afternoon it was announced that the petitioner (Mr. Isaacson, the Conservative candidate) had a majority of one vote. The inquiry, however, is not concluded. CoAGui.orE.—Cement for Broken Articles, 6d. Is, 2s; postage 2nd. Sold everywhere. Kay, Bros., Stockport.—Advt. PEERS IN THE DOCK.—At Lambeth Police Court on Tues- day Lord Hinton (son of Earl Poulett) was committed, in company with two other persons, for trial on a charge of obtaining goods by false pretences. At Guildhall Police Court Lord Graves (an Irish peer) and W. E. Kepner were remanded on charges of fraud. DANGEROUS HABIT—At Swansea, John Buxton, an aged sea captain, has been in the habit of placing a lighted can- dle on his pillow on going to bed. On Monday night, after he had fallen asleep, the candle set fire to the bedclothes and•curtains, and, on the landlady perceiving the smoke and , going into the bedroom, she found that Captain Buxton had been suffocated. BEETIIAM A Sox, Chemists, Cheltenham.—Advt. RAILWAY COLLISION.—A serious collision occurred on the Lancashire Railway at Cliviger, near Burnley, on Monday morning. Whilst a goods train which had been shunted was leaving a siding it was ran into by another fast luggage train from Normanton. The engines, which met, were thrown off the line and greatly damaged ; a number of waggons fell over the embankment and were smashed, and their csntents were scattered about. Fortunately no one was seriously hurt by the collision, which caused a total , stoppage of traffic for some hours.

TELE Biiroswr. EXECUTIONER—Sir Claude C. de Cree- pigny. of Heybridge, near Maldon, has acknowledged that he acted as Berry's assistant at the triple execution of the Netherby Hall burglars on the Bth inst. at Carlisle. Sir Claude s4ys he could not order a man to do what he was afraid of doing himself, and as he might be Sheriff of Essex someday he should like to be able to undertake an execution if Berry should be engaged else- where. He pinioned Baker on the morning of the execution while Berry performed the same operation upon Martin and Badge. NATIONAL RIFLE ASSOCIATION.—The annual meeting of the National Rifle Association was held in London, on Wednesday, under the presidency of the Duke of Cam- bridge. There was a large attendance. His Royal High- ness said that although the association was in a prosperous position, great difficulty was experienced in getting good ranges owing to the expense. His Roy al Highness an- nounced that the new solid cartridge would be used in future at Wimbledon, in order to avid jamming. He re- erretted that Australia and India would not be represented this year. EXECUTION AT KNITTSFORD.—A farm labourer named Owen M'Gill, who was sentenced to death at Chester Assizes for murdering his wife, was hanged on Monday morning at Knuteford prison. The crime was one of unusual brutality the woman having been literally kicked and beaten to death by her husband. No effort was made to obtain a mitigation of the sentence, and any such attempt would probably have failed in view of Lord Coleridge's description of the crime as a "most serious murder." :14'G-ill walked firmly to the scaffold, and when the drop fell he died instantaneously. Berry was the executioner. AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS' ALLOTMENTS.—Lord Eldon has recently laid out a considerable portion of agricultural land on his Dorset estate as allotment gardens for the work- ing classes. At a small village called Herston several acres have been set apart for this purpose, and the allotments have been very rapidly taken up. The land is among the best on the estate, and has been tilled for several years by some of the largest farmers in the neighbourhood. Mr. G. Burt, another large landowner in the same neichbonr- hood, has also laid out large plots of land as allotments at the ground rent of 25s per annum or the freehold at £25 per acre.

• THE DRIFTING OF THE COLUMBINE.—The.WOMan, Eliza- beth Mouat, who was cast ashore in the smack Columbine, arrived at Hull on Tuesday morning, in the steamer Domingo, from Bergen. Mr. C. H. Wilson, M.P., bad in- structed that she should have a free passage from any port at waich the steamer might touch. She left Hull by tee eight o'clock train for the North. A communication was received at Hull from a place of amusement, offering her liberal terms for an engagement. Miss Monat saierthat be- fore she decided on anything she would go home and see her friends. She had with her many presents in money and clothes made to her in Norway. SOUTHPORT AND CHESHIRE LINES EXTENSION RAILWAY. —The seventh ordinary half-yearly general meeting of the , shareholders of the Southport and Cheshire Lines Extension ; Railway, was held on Saturday, at the Company's offices, Lord-street Station, Southport, Mr. David Ratcliffe, of Formby, near Liverpool, the deputy chairman, presiding. ! The report and balance sheet were adopted. The two re- tiring directors were Mr. Thomas J.P.. of , Ince Blundell, near Liverpool, and Mr. David Radcliffe, JP., of Formby Hall, Formby. To fill their places on the board the following gentlemen were -elected :—Mr. George Gilroy, CE,, of the Woodlands, Gathurst, and Wigan, and Mr. Robert Musgrave Craven, surgeon, of Southport. Thanks to the chairman closed the meeting. ASSOCIATION OF CHAMBERS or COMMERCE.—The annual meeting of the Association of Chambers of Commerce was opened on Tuesday in Westminster Town Hall, London, Mr. Norwood presiding. Mr. B. Samueleon, M.P., was elects president for the ensuing year. A resolution recommending a policy of retaliation towards those countries which did not grant the British goods the terms conceded to the most favoured nation was negatived after an animated discussion, in which the Spanish Government was plainly referred to as the object of the resolution, and in which the principles I of Free Trade and Protection was brought forward It was ' resolved to urge the Foreign Office to re-open negotiations witle the Spanish Government with a view to obtaining "most favoured nation" treatment for this country. The association expressed a hope, in the form of a resolution, that the Royal Commission would obtain viva voce evidence as to the causes of trade depression. BREACH OF PROMISE.—ABOUT 2,000 LOVE LETTERS.— Lord Traynor and a jury have tried in the Court of Sessions. Edinburgh, an action for £l,OOO damages for alleged breach of promise of marriage, at the instance of Jane Swan, St. George's road, Glasgow, against John Haddow, a brewer's traveller, residing at Windsor-street, New City-road. Glas- gow. The promise of marriage was said to have been made in January, 1874, but in 1883 he married another woman. Pursuer, who gave her evidence in a cheerful manner, and frequently joined in the laughter which her statements elicited, said she was 43 years of age. Defendant lodged with her mother for a twelvemonth from June, 1873. In August of last year her mother was at Ardrossan, and she kept house, when defendaßt began to pay attention to her. They were in the kitchen alone when he spoke to her first of marriage. Silo did not then eccept him, bat on a Sunday forenoon in the park he again proposed marriage, and she accepted him. He spoke of the marriage taking place during his helidays in the summer of 1874, but sub- sequently he asked, owing to his mother's illness, that their marriage should be postponed till January, 1875, and a week or two afterwards he asked her to postpone their mar- riage for six years. She said," Well this is rather unrea- sonable," and he then suggested five years. She agreed to that, and for five years saw him nearly every day, and cor- responded regularly with him. In 1880 she wrote to him to meet her at the West End Park. She wished to speak to him about carrying out his premise. She went to the park, and saw him coming up on the other side of the street with his arm round a girl's waist. He took no notice of her, and when she called to him he waved his hand. She followed, and said to him, " Are you not ashamed of yourself ?" He took no notice of her, and then she said to the woman." Do you know that this is not a free man ?" The woman re- plied that she knew all. In 1883 defender married this girl. —Defender, called as a witness on his own behalf, said be was 32 years of aee. He never courted Miss Swan. It was from her friends that he first heard of marriage, and that stetement made him leave her mother's lodgings. In Jan., 1874, he was 19 years of age.—Counsel : Did you ever get any letters from her ?—Witness: Oh, about 2000., (Laugh- ter.) He was eegaged to hie wife for about eight years.— The jury, after a few minutes' ebsence,retunied a unanimous verdict for the defender. div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 27, 1868.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 27, 1868.

"LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL must be judged by himself, and neither his utterances nor his actions with regard to the Irish, question are such as to inspire confidence.' This is the language not of a Liberal journal —not even of the Standard," which some time ago gave his lordship a piede of its mind—but of that ultra-Tory organ "The Morning Post." It would seem that the Tory party are getting tired of dancing attendance upon a political will-o'-the-wisps who cannot do more than lead them from one quagmire to another. Great things were expected of his cultivation of that plant known as Tory-Democracy; and it was con- sidered a clever move on his part to " dish the Whigs " by out-bidding them last year in making terms with Mr. PA RNELL. The better-minded amongst the Conservatives certainly shook their heads at this kind of manceuvring ; but the party as a party were ready to do anything which would give theta a majority at the General Election. Accord- ingly, they angled for and obtained the Irish vote—but, alas for their hopes, they failed to get a majority. As nothing succeeds like.suc- cess, so nothing fails like failure. The Tories were disgusted with themselves, and finding they must fall, instead of rewarding the Parnellites, they vented their spleen upon them by intimating their intention, if the opportunity were given them, of bringing in a bill to suppress the National League. There is an end, therefore, of the Tory- Parnellite alliance, and we are not sorry that Mr. PARNELL has been "rounded on." He ought to have known better than trust his natural enemy ; it was a bad arrangement from beginning to end, and good could not possibly come of it. Lord RANDor_px CHURCHILL, leavinc, his new love, has gone back to his old leaving hatred of the Nationalists of Ireland. He has this week been beating the big drum for the Orange- men of Ulster, but being out of practice with this particular music, he has sought to make up by extra noise, what he obviously lacked in precision. Lord RANDOLPH raises the old cry " The battle of the Boyne, and no surrender ;" and now that his lord- ship has given the cue, perhaps Sir GILBERT GREENALL and his friends will be less anxi- ous to repudiate it than they were in Novem- ber last. The Catholics then were common friends, working with them in a common cause; now —judging from the Belfast speeches—they are, as of yore, uncommonly like enemies. Mr. GLADSTONE is denounced for having done so much to rid Ireland of her grievances, for" disestablishing the Irish Church," for "breaking the power of the Irish landlords" (in other words passing the Land Act), and for seeking to turn Dublin Univer- sity "into a Roman Catholic seminary." The Orangemen of Ulster cheered all this—just as they cheered the following attack which Lord RANDOLPH made upon the clergy of Ireland and upon the confessional : And there is something very bad in the connec- tion between the local Catholic clergymen and the local branches of the National League. Of course, from the peculiar practice of the Church of Rome, many of the priests who take an active part in this agitation must know of the connection between the local branches of the League and some of the most frightful forms of crime and outrage. (Pro- longed applause.) We would ask Catholic priests in this part of the country, who used their influence on be- half of the Tories at the last election, whether they are content to accept the Tory leader as their spokesman on this question— whether we ate to regard it as a true state- ment of the facts of the ease as to Ireland that " there is something very bad in the connection between the Leal Catholic clergy- men and the local branches of the National League ?" Let them speak out, for, if they do not, they cannot complain that judgment goes against them by default. But it is not the clergy alone; the Par- nellites are put upon their trial. Three months ago they voted Tory to please Lord RANDOLPH 'and his 'friends, and this is what his lordship has to say of them : The forces which Mr. Parnell directs emanate from the basest prejudices of class and sect, forces which are kept together by means of appeals to covetousness and greed, and by terms held out to them of the acquisition of property by plunder, violence, and fraud. (Cheers.) It would be interesting to learn what the Nationalists of Waning-ton. Widnr-s, and St. Helens think of ibis choice description of them. They voted for the Tory candidate in each of these places; they were the means, it is not too much to of a Tor) in each

div.p: ------- Insiante 'being returned. If they are not wholly sttisfied with the portraiture of the Tory leader they should say so, as their silente may be taken for acquiesence. They am not usually dumb when trodden on; but Perhaps they like to lick the hand of his lord- ship ? They will not, however, be permitted to remain in the submissive mood, unless they are willing to be knocked all to pieces. Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL has. had enough of Seen Mr. ly-shallyi he wants to fight. He has not GLADSTONE'S scheme for dealing With Ireland, but he knows all about it, and has come te• the conclusion beforehand that I,t "must inevitably, if carried to a success- MI issue, not only dissolve the connection tweet Ireland and Great Britain, but must shatter the British Empire." He is not, of ourse, going to stand by and see the British ..inpire shattered without making an effort to iave it. Privileges which are worth demon- strating for are worth fighting for, and when the time comes " when the combat I ;:teepens"—Lord:RANnoLPH will be there—if 1 41e is not elsewhere. All this looks, to be ' very absurd when put forth as the Con- servative policy for dealing with Ireland. Nlishmen can afford to laugh at it, but, as, it affects Ulster, the matter has a serious lide. It is an appeal to " Loyalists" to show , !heir regard for QUEEN and country by becom- ing disloyal; it is a direct incitement to rebellion: and if Lord RANDOLPH CHURCH- ILI, does not mind what he is about he may b 1 e called upon to take a place in the pri- soner's dock besides BURNS, and CHAMPION, aud HYNDMAN. "The Morning Post" may. Well say that "neither his utterances nor his actions with regard to the Mai question are Stich as to inspire confidence."

WARRINGTON is determined not to be behind di feeding ttie hungry, for there has been a ready response to the appeal for aid on behalf 13,f. the unemployed. The two meetings which Rave been held have resulted in a number of Practical suggestions, some of them wisely , In, the direction of taking precautions against °use of the funds. The Committee which Is now actively at work cannot be too f ca,reful in seeing to it that what they give is tven to the deserving poor—to those who ! .ve struggled honestly against a hard fate. :,4eY will not find the families of this s'a,ss amongst those who are clamorous for b.rei_def- They will want seeking out, for people 'no have never been "on the parish" re ther "ish to hide than lay bare their poverty. As Tr the intemperate, idle, and ne'er-do-well, I:'e3' should be left '.to shift for themselves. , ("oor rates are paid in order that this class illay not starve, and they have no claim what- e, 'ler on such a fund as is now being raised 'cl relieve the unemployed. It may be, as the ; 'IA:YOR states, that the ladies who have been I at work have shown themselves exceedingly .Pathetic ; but there is a danger of sym- Pathy having too much play. If experience; ltn the distribution of alms has taught one I .ning more clearly than another it is that ; I,ndiscriminate relief is no relief at all ; that I lt aggravates the very evils it is intended to ;and that it is therefore a positive injury 1 • society. If there were fewer persons in the gabit of disposing of every beggar who pre- 4ents himself by giving him a copper, there I would be fewer tramps and fewer crimi- The habitual loafer would be driven , 10 the conclusion that a meal must be earned Defore it can be eaten; and in good times, 'at any rate, the streets would be free of the Policeman's pest. It is altogether different With the man who has only half work or no ; work at all, and who is doing all he can to ake both ,ends meet and keep his "bits o' zings together. He is a brother on life's i°,,• ad, and should have a Jift on the way—a Which he should be able to recognise as ii!elPful without being in the least degree humi- lating. It is not thought there is as large a „ , ,'ercentage of this class in Warrington as in „llne other towns, where there is less variety ! Manufactures ; but as to this we shall , tlow more when the investigators have ~,c°nlpleted their rounds. Be they few or 'anY, we are quite sure that the benevolence °f the borough will be equal to the emer- .gency.

If Warrington will have a Chamber of Corn - ,T,llerce, why don't the members attend? .here were five persons present at the meet- ing held on Monday—including the hon. secretaries.

The Socialist leaders are justified in corn- Iblaining of the cartoon in Punch last week, 'which represented them as being hanged in ounishment of their crime. Apart from the 'ase being sub judiet, it was an outrage on Pod taste of which our leading comic I°llrnal is, happily, not often guilty.

They have been having an Irish Fair at t. 141 elens--not an Irish row, for there would be novelty in that. After having the changes on Sale of Work, Bazaar, and Christ- V4l Tree, Irish Fair sounds very well. It till do—always assuming that "a taste c't the shillalv " is left out of the pro- gramme.

,•It has been suggested that 1887—the `°lllnlencement of the fiftieth year of the ?,tlten% reign—should be celebrated as the ti_ar of Jubilee. Her Majesty, it is stated, jlinks.it is better to wait till the full circle of h%le half century is completed. The Golden k'vedding of Monarch and Subject may then ve celebrated with perfect fitness.

The recovery of Mr. Latham, M.P. for the \-rewe Division of Cheshire, from the illness ."41, hich at one time threatened to prove fatal, a matter of heart-felt satisfaction. Mr. tharn has gone to Southport for a month, "btld hopes in the course of sir weeks or so to t able to assist other advanced 'Liberals . the good work they are doing in Paxlia- '"Ent.

' ..'le Tory p ry Lave no sense of gratitude. Qi ally, t ev ewarded the Nationalists

r for support given them at the last election by setting about the suppression Of the National League ; locally, they have this week rewarded the Roman Catholics for their services by objecting to Catholic priests voting, as heretofore, for members of the Board of Guardians. Before the General Election, the Tory party had nothing but caresses for the Catholics; now they have nothing but kicks.

It would be a goad thing for the unem- ployed, and a good thing for Warrington, if ad- vantage were taken of the present depres- sion in trade to raise the chimneys of the various manufactories. They are, for the most part, about half the height they ought to be. Warrington lying low, and with its chimneys low, is, for its size, one of the most smoke-smitten towns in the kingdom.

What a god-send it would be if the Ship Canal Works could be immediately com- menced ! Every effort should be made to expedite the passing of the bill for enabling the company to pay interest out of capital while the canal is in course of construction. After being beaten on the main issue, the opposition would do well to retire from a struggle which cannot do good, but may do harm by causing delay.

Just now there are labourers who hay. walked hundreds of miles in search of em- ment. They are continually going to and from Preston and Southport, where in the one case they are making new docks, and in the other a new railway. A poor fellow named Shores, who had tramped through the f'otter- ies, broke down near St. Helens on Monday, and had to be taken to the workhouse hos- pital in a semi-p tralysed condition. It is hard, this going about—begging, as Burns has it, a brother of the earth to give him leave to toil.

A story is going the round that " a Brad- ford gentleman" has been denounced as an imposter, and turned out of a public-house at Heywood for tendering a "spurious five- pound note" in payment for." drinks round" He tried an oyster man, who went for a policeman. Ultimately the suspect was locked up, and it was then found that the note was 'a perfectly good one. The times must be very bad; tradesmen now-a-days don't know a Bank ot England note when they see one.

Mr. Peter Rylands, M.P., has given no- tice in the House of Commons to move on March sth: " That the right of sitting in the House of Lards possessed by certain bishops of the Church of England is con- trary to public policy, injurious to religious interests, and ought to be abolished." Mr. Rylands is on the right track. History enables him to make out a strong .case against the bishops. It will alike astound and disgust those who are not familiar with the facts to learn how consistent their lord- ships have been in doing evil, and that con- tinually.

The ancestors of Lord Randolph Churchill must be a bad lot when Lord Castlereagh is singled out by him for mention. His repu- tation is an evil one. „Byron wrote of him contemptuously as "that long spout of blood and water leaden Castlereagh." Shelley in his " Masque of Anarchy" thus refers to him :
I met Murder on the way— He had a mask like Castlereagh; Very smooth he looked, yet grim, Seven bloodhounds followed him.
This is hard-hitting, but there was occasion for it. It is to be hoped we shall soon see the last of the Castle government of the Castlereaghs.

Child stealing seems to be treated as a light offence by. the Eddisbury magistrates. Two hawkers—a man and wife named Williams, who have no children of their own —took away from Kingsley the child, aged ten years, of a Ikbourer named Clarke. They kept possession of it until they found the police were on their track, and then they sent the child home. It does not appear that the little girl had been ill-treated, and it was alleged that the father had said they could take hr away at any time. The Chairman, "good easy man," thought they might ldok over the case this time on payment of costs. It was only a child that had been abducted; if it had been a hare, or a pheasant, some one would have had to go to gaol.

LECTURE AT WIDNES.—Mr. J. B. ison on Monday evening delivered a lecture on " Turning points in English Church history" to a moderate audience. The Vicar pre- sided. • CONCERT AT WIDNES.—A moderate audience assembled in the National Schools, Waterloo-road, on Wednesday even- ing, to listen to a concert given in aid of the Widnes Pro- testant Drum and Fife • Band. The Vicar presided. The band performed several selections in a praiseworthy manner, and Mr. A. Short, of Liverpool, caused nauCh amusement by his ventriloquial .sketches. Mr. J. Stirk gave a cornet solo, and Mr. Gordon a violin solo. EVANGELISTIC SERVICES.—Mr. and Mrs. Henry Wiggan, London Evangelists, and the Rev. J. Calvert are now hold- ing very interesting einging Evangelistic services in the `l.'rimitive Methodist Chapel, Hatchinson-street. Mr. Lewis. with a choir and instrumentalists numbering over 70, leads .the people in songs. Mr. Wigizari's hymn and tune books are used. The solos by several young ladies on Sunday were very popular. All the meetings were impressive, and at the night service a number of peksons publicly professed to be converted. Mr. W. ,C ix, of St. Helens, tools part with Mr. and Mrs. Wiggan on Sunday. Mr. and Mrs. Wig- gm are announced to hold :eimilar services in Warrington after they close at Widnes. NEW .CILUECIT, GILEENWAT-ROAD, EUNCORN.--ThE sixth entertainment of the series was provided on Thursday even- ing,.by Mr. John B. Raison, and other Widnes friends. Mr. J. W. Liglatburn presided over a moderate audience. The glee party rendered in a tastehel manner the glees, "When winds breathe soft," "The pearl divers," and "Sleep, gentle lady." The lady vocalist was Miss Jameson, whose Pinging watea decided treat to the audience, each of her songs." The nightingale's triil " and "The Chcassian'e dream," being re-demanded. Mr. Imison sang in excellent lityle the beau- tiful sacred sang, "Remember now thy Creatar," and as an encore song • gave "An Englishman am I." "Norah, the pride of Kildare," was tastefnlly rendered by Mr. Large, while the hurnourous aona,s of Mr. F. Scott and Mr. T. Davies provoked great merriment. Mr. S. Jessop gave two piccolo solos. Mrs. Callander was the accompanist. THE IRISH QUESTION must engage much of the time of the present Parliament, and there is no doubt that Ireland has suffered under great injus- tice, not the least of which is that miserable foreign stale limed eggs are constantly sold as the product of our Sister Isle. This injustice and wrong to Ire- land can best.• be remedied by buying Lever's Fresh Eggs, which are received daily from Poultry Farms in Ulster, and are guaranteed Fresh and. New Laid.
