RUNCORN COFFEE AND COCOA HOUSE COMPANY.—On Monday evening the eighth annual meeting of the share- holders of thus Company was held at their premises, High- street. Mr. J. 0. Jackson occupied the chair, and there were present Messrs. J. Simpson, S. C. Beckett, R. Norman, J. Weadoweroft, T. Higgin, T. W. Speak.man, and B. Knive- ton (secretary). The report stated that the receipts from refreshments amounted to £930 12e 4d, and Vie net profits to £B9 18s 10d. out of which the directors recommended a payment of a dividend of 5 per cent. in paid-up capital, and carry forward a balance of .£5 17s 4d. Amongst the items of expenditure were wages £137 us Bd, gas £33 ss, coal £29 3s 10d, and rates and taxes £l6 193 7d.—Tbe Chair- mate expressed his pleasure at the fact that the corrlpanv could pay a dividend of 5 per cent. He thought that next year they would be in even a better posltion. They had been peyiag off a part of their borrowed money, and now : they were only paying interest on £450. They were also . paying a leas rate of interest, so that their worst times were gone. Their receipts were improving, and there was every prospect of their continuing so, while they were at the same time reducing their expenses and liabilities, The company was formed, not only as a Profitable investment, but in the hope that something might be doe to lessen drunkenness. (Hear, hear.) He thought they had succeeded to a consider- able extent in carrying out that object. The men ern:tic:and by the Bridgewater Navigation Contpeny used the Company's rooms far the parpoee of dividing their money instead of meeting as they formerly did in public house... where they spent money in drink. (Hear, hear.) On the motion of Mr. Speakman, seconded by Mr. Higgin, the report was adopted.— 'hid Rev. Canon Barclay and 'Mr. J. Meadowcrof t Were unanimously re-elected directors. Mr. Becket said last year had been one of great depression, and all who had atly- thing to do with shipping were aware that they had nothing like the number of vessels in the docks that they had had in previous years. This hid affected the receipts of the corn • pene-, but he believed they bed got over the depression and might look forward to next year with great hope.

BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL , CHAPEL, RUNCORN. In connection with this place of worship the annual t-a party took place in the Schoolroom. Vicar-street, on Tues- day evening. A good number sat down to tea. Subsequently a public meeting was held under the presidency of the Rev. J. D. Thomas, the pastor. In opening the proceedings, the Chairman delivered a brief address in 'which he gave a word of welcome to those present, and expressed a hope that the members of the congregation would on that occasion resolve to do better in the future than they had done in the past. He made a reference to the forthcoming,. revivalist services that were to be conducted by Mr. J. Green, the Warwick- shire Evangelist. Alluding to the bazaar it is proposed to hold in a few months, he observed that they would have to ask the help of outsiders in that effort, and he most say that he bad never found the people of other denominations backward to sympathize with them in their undertakings. By united and hearty action he hoped they would find that at the close of the year the debt on the l‘lanse was cleared away and a good balance in hand with which to do some very necessary repairs to the chapel. The Rev. James Johnson, of Preseot, then delivered a speech. We were living at a time when everythivg around us was full of agitation and fraught with great consequ- ences, and they who were part of Christ's church could not feel too deeply their responsibilities, and strive earnestly to , discharge the trust Jesus Christ had imposed upon them. Men asked for more learned teaching in the church for, amusement, science, and the ideas of statesmen and sound reformers. The church did not exist for that puroose. Her mission was to bring men tegether that they might worship God in sincerity and in trath ; that they might utter their prayers an petitions, and listen to the everlast- ing Word. The power of the church lay in sanetifiedliyes 4nd in holy deeds. He urged those present to he shining lights of purity, truth, and holiness around all the turmoi▪ l and tumult of the times. (Applause.) The Rev- W. L. Roberts, of Liverpool, then addresseda few remarks. Alluding to the evangelistic services, he sai▪ d we looked upon our churches as schemes for raising nieney i to support somebody else to do its work. The churches, ▪ n fact, had get to be a sort of one-man concern by a vase majority of people, and the members of the congregations %looked up-.;n their hare of the work as what they could do

to stimulate the pastors, the deacons, and the teachers—that they had done their part when they had contributed their mite and shown their sympathy. Each one—all Christian men and women ought to look out for their own particular department in order to make God's work more successful, and bring forth fruit to the honour and glory of the Lord Jesus Christ. (Applause.) The Rev. W. Jones, of Chester, also spoke upon the inspir- ing principle of Christianity. Mr. F. Beck proposed a vote of thanks to the speakers, the choir, which had rendered several pieces of music under the leadership of Mr. Ravenscroft. and the ladies who had provided the tea. In doing so he pointed out that for years past they had always had a balauce in band at the end of the year. Last year had been an excepion, and there was a deficiency of £l2 tia id. This was accounted for by the fact that they had lost such a large number of frien.ts by removals and by death. A system was to be adoieed to raise the money requisite. Mr. Wyllie seconded the motion, end urged the import- ance of the young people taking an active part in the church and school.
It was carried by acclamation, and the meeting con- cluded.

MILTON CO • GREGATIONAL CHAPEL, In IDNES. In connection with this place of worship, the annual tea party was held in the chapel on Thursday evening. Ab-ut 200 persons partook of the repast provided, the following ladies presiding at the tables :—Mesdatnee fillips, Yeas- dale, Lewis, Bray, Wilkinson, Chapman, and Doming ; sod Misses Travis, Warne, J. Warne, Baron, Arid A. Travis. The subsequent proceedings were presided over by Mr. Eustace Carey, who expressed his pleasure at being present that evening, and it was a still greater pleasure to see such a large audience. From inquiries he had made of Mr. Hughes, ha was glad to be able to congratulate them on the fact that the congregation was increasing, that the church members were increasing, and that the scholars were in- creasing in a very satisfactory manner. He warned them not to rely so much as congregations usually did upon the sole and unaided efforts of their minister, and be spoke very favourably of the system adopted in America in conducting their services. They were not satisfied with three or four hymns, a prayer, and A long sermon, but bad all sorts of excellent music, amid whatever they thought would please the people. ~.at Mr. Ward Beecher's church they had all kinds of sriEiat gatherings, such as they had there that evening, and he thought they ought to have more of then:. He was quite sure they might do a great deal more tnan they did to make their chapel ' more attractive. He conciuded with an appropriate refer- ence to the death Of the Kew. Hugh Stwhl Brown, of Liverpool.—The cor cer t was then proceeded with. Songe were given by Mrs. Poole, Miss Jones (Runcorn), !Wise F. Travis, Miss A. 'Levis ; Messrs. F. Wilkinson, Morris, J. Littler, J. R. Lea. and J. Powell. Miss Travis and Mr. E. L. Warne performed a march, wan° ann cencertina, and Miss L. Wilkinson gave a pianoforte solo. Before the meeting separated. the Chairman moved the following resolution,which had been drawn up by the Rev. R. Hughes, the pastor :—" That the congregation of Milton-street Independent Chapel, Widnee, being assembled at ite annual meeting, hears with deep sorrow of the decease of the Rev. H. Stowell Brown. an., desire to offer sincere y 'sympath to Mr. Brown's family." The resolution was carried unani- mously.

div.head: RUNCORN WAFERWORKS COMPANY
div.p: RUNCORN WAFERWORKS COMPANY

The half-yearly inesting of the shareholders of the Run- corn, Weston, and Helton Waterworks Company was held on Monday, at the Public Hall, Runcern. Mr. J. B.undrit, J.P., chairman of the Boa, d of Directors, presided, and there were present Mez,ers. W Hayes, J. Simpiore Bankee, Timmins, W. Whitteker, P. Smith, Jones Straw, and W. F. Selkeld (secretary.) Tbe repo: tof the direc (es ,tared diet the revenue arc .unt shuvreei a balance of £6BB lie 10, in- cluding £lB 5s bright from the helf-e ear, out ef which 'he directors recommend a dividend to tie declared of £3 10a per cent. per annum, free from income tax, payable on and after the first day of Match. This would absorb £525, leaving a bala,nce of £lO3 lie 101 to be carried forward. The plant and buildings were all in good order, the supply of water is abundant and of excellent quality. Oering te. the steppage of the smelting works and the glycerine won ha, the con- sumption of water lately had been considerably less than when they were in operation, hut cher,: was every pro.- ability of of the demand being increased in future from. other places. The Chairman, in moving the aloption of the report and passing of accounts, said the continued depteesion in trade had had a bad effect on the company, and the closing of the smelting works and the glycerine works had made a difference in their receipts of between £4OO and £-00 a year. This was a serious item when it was remembeied that the pumping and other expenses went on just as usual. Tiler was now, however, a hreght.-r prospect ['he Run- corn Soap and Alkali Company were taking a larger quan- tity of water, and the d,rec!ors hoped they would continue to do se. Owing to the depression', r litre were more empty houses than at this time last year, wb!ch bad also dirnie- ished the consumption of water. Lest year their pipes were connected with 4 022 houses in Runcorn, Weston, and Halton ; 370 of those houses were empty. At the end of 1835 their pipes were connected with 4,050 houses, but the number of empties bad increased to 460. All this tended to keep down their rev'enue. He was glad to say they bad made a goed contract for ceals during the coming year, which would materially reduce their ,expenditure both in price cud carting from ,the station.. This would benefit ! the compaey to a considerable extent.—Mr. Bankes secou- dee! the motion which was adopted.—On the proposition of Mr. Shaw, seconded by Mr. P. Smith, a vote of thanks was accorded to the chairmen and directors.—Mr. eayesalle,red in terms of regret to the death of Mr. Norman, Mr. Nor- man was invariably present at their meetings, and he (Mr. Hayes) was extremely sorry that he was not with them on that occasion, ,(Hear, beer).
RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. APPO!N Mk:NT OF CHAIRMAN.

A special meeting of the Runcorn Board of Improvement Commissioners was held at the. Town Hall, Waterloo-road, on Thursday morning, for the purpose of electing a chair- man in place of Mr. It ,bert Shaw, resigned. There were present—Mems. Speakman. Dobson, Grice, Itnison, Mellor, Timmins, Harris, White, Taylor, Lake, Fisher, Lighthurn, and Ntarshall (secretary).—The Secretary took the chair, and explained that accerding to tbe Commissioners Clauses Act the person appointed to fill the position of chairman wonld remain in office so long as the retiring chairman would have continued to act.—Mr. Dobson proposed that Mr. P. Speakman be appointed chairman. He was an old member, understood the business of the Board, and he had no doubt that if he were appointed he would prove himself worthy of the confidence they reposed in him —Mr.Timmins asked bow Mr. Shaw had tendered his resignation as chair- mate—The Secretary replied that it had not been delivered I in writing., but there was not the sliehtest doubt he had re- signed.—Mr. Timmins seconded the proposition. Mr. Speakman. he said, would make a good chairman. Every- one was aware of his abilities and the great attention be had devoted to the affairs of the town, and he (Mr. Tim- ' mins) thought they could not do better than appoint Mr. Speakman i .—Mr. Lightburn, n supporting the motion, expressed regret that the appointment should have to be made before the time had expired; It was a great pity that an honest divergence of opin- ion on one or two subjects should have put the Board is the position in which they wets now placed, when they agreed with the chairman in the majority of points.-Ihe resolution was carried unanim- ously.—Mr. Speakman then took the chair, and said he could hardly find words to express his gratitude for the unanimous way in which they had appointed him chairnlan that day. He regretted, with Mr. Lightburn, that the posi- tion should have to be filled up before the natural time had occurred, but so it was, and he asked the Board to help him during the remainder of the period in conducting the busi- ness of the Board. The business of the Board could only be carried on by true unanimity‘of feeling in the members, and if there was that feeling he was sure that The future of the Board would be a happy one to all the ny.mbers. He thanked them very much for the honour they had conferred upon him, and he hoped his services would prove him worthy of the confidence they had reposed in him that morning.—The meeting then terminated.
WESLEYAN MUSICAL FESTIVAL AT RUNCORN.

The third annual musical festival in connection with the Brunswick Wesleyan Sunday School took place on Monday evening in Runcorn Public Hall. -There was a capital at- tendance.— In the absence of Mr. R. Shaw, through' indis- position, the Rev. G. Wood occupied the chair, and a brief address said the success of the former festivals had been such as to include their friende to contemplwe making that an annual gathering. It was well known, he dared Fray, that Brunswick Sunday School was the oldest institution of its kind in the town, and that in the past it had contri- buted very largely to the moral and religious welfare of the , young of the town. It was doing good service in the ' same matter at the present time. Any surplus from that festival would be appropriated towards the interests of the school. The programme was then proceeded with. The first part consisted of the cantata "Jesus of Nazareth," and it was rendered by a choir of 300 voices, in a mariner that won the gratified commendation of all present. The voices were well balanced, ani aided by the services of an lent - lent orchestral band, were harmonious ' and powerful. Mr. J.H. Harrison sang the recitative "Jesus the carpenter," and was associated with Messrs. Kent. Morris, Fox, and Miss Smith, Miss Simkin, and Miss Beckett in several quartettes and other concerted pieces, which were all examples of careful vocalisation. Mr. A. Fox, whose voice was full and rich as ever, scored the first encore of the evening is the recitative and chorus " The miracles." The air "Christ chooses His disciples" was given by Mr. Morris in capital fashion, and his interpretstion of "The believers' song" was much enjoyed. Miss Jones acquitted herself in the various pieces set down to her name with intelligence and taste, and Miss Simkin met with a deserved success. In the second part Miss Jones gave in admirable style several 'recitatives from Handel's Messiah, followed by tha chorus "Glory to God," rendered with pawer and precision by the choir. The anthems " Welcome to the children," and the " Christian mariner's hymn " were also given. Hearty plaudits from all parts of the audience rewarded Mr. J. H. Harrison for a tuneful and spirited rendering of " Ann, arm, ye brave." A pretty piece of vocalisation WAS the song; "Children's voices," by Miss Smith (of Leigh), the con- cealed chorus adding much to the general eff..ct. An en- thusiastic recall was the result. Cowen's charming song "The reaper and the flowers" received artistic treatment at the hands of Mr. Moors. The solo part in Handel's " 0 'llicu that tellest "was given with much expression by Miss Sitnkin. The performances of the band were not the least

div.p: MASONIC SERVICE AT RUNCORN.

Runcorn Parish Church was the scene of a very interest- ing service on Wednesday evening. By pre mission of the Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A., who was pres-nt. the Freemasons of the Ellesmere Lodge, No. 758, had arranged the service, which was for the good and lauduable object of aiding the funds of the Cheshire Eelucational Masonic Institution. The interest was, h•wever, loc the fact that the lodge are about to apply to that excellent ii,s itation for a grant towards the education and support of the three children, of the late Mr. William Houghton, who was tyler to the Elles- mere Lodge and apparitor to the Parish Church. Conse- quently the sacred edifice was almost filled with a sympa- thetid congregation, where the Masons attired in all the symbols of their order, walked down the aisle to the places reserved for them. div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Thursday, Mr. T. S. Tin-lulls presiding. Present—the Revs. Father Clarke, and Father Finegan, Messrs. Bradshaw, Brock, Deacon, Imison, Glover, Robinson, and Danby (clerk).

div.head: WELCOME.
div.p: A WELCOME.
The Chairman, on behalf of the members, gave Mr. Robinson a hearty welcome to a seat at the Board, and ex- pressed great aatisfaction that he had been able to accept the nominai ion.

DISTRICT EDCCATION. The District Education Committee reported that daring January (three weeks) there were 179 applications for the payment of fees, and 155 parsons appeared before the com- mittee for contravention of the Education Act. Fees were recommended to be paid in 172 cases. Twenty persons were convicted before the magistrates.—The minutes were passed on tbe motion of Mr. Deacon.

div.head: FRYE DINNERS TO SCHOOL CHILDREN.
div.p: FRYE DINNERS TO SCHOOL CHILDREN.

The School Management Committpe reported that they had had an application from Mr. H. Wade Deac in for the use of a room at the Warrington-road and West Bank Schools, in which to supply free dinners for a thort time to those Board school children who need them. The commit- tee had granted the free use of the rooms to Mr. Deacon. with the understanding that a small charge would be made for the fuel used in cooking the fool.---Mr. Davies moved the passing of the minute. He thought the Board indebted to Mr. Deacon and his friends for making this offer. Is doing this work Mr. Deacon and those who were assisting him were consulting the welfare of the children, and therefore the interests of the sclabols.—At the request of the Chairman, Mr. Dea- con made a few remarks. Some time ago they would remember Messrs. Stringer and Sadler tried to wart a free breakfast movement. That movement did not suceeet for various reasons. He (Mr. Deacon) subsequently made in- quiries. which satisfied him that there was a considerabie number of children in the Board schools who really re- quired food. He made an estimate of the cost of providing free dinners • for a few weeks, and his friends kindly sub- scribed the amount wanted. The children had been fed for more than a month, and he had sufficient money to go on for three or four weeks longer. He only required rooms At West Bank and Warrington-road because he had made ar- rangements at Simm's Cross for dinners to be provided out- side the schools. The food was not costly; it was cooked economically, and he went round unexpectedly occasionally to try what it was like. He was very much obliged to the bead masters for the trouble they had taken in connection with the movement. The mistresses had also boen rry good in serving the dinners, so that the cost was very little indeed. Mr. Stringer had sent subscriptions to the schools on his own account perfectly independently of him (M. r. Deacon), and he had no responsibility in connection with those funds.—The Chairman remarked that they were all very mach obliged to Mr. Deacon. .He was done?... a great- deal of good by feedimr these poor cfnldrem.--.M-. Deacon : lam not in it alone, Mr. ChairtnAn.—The Chairman : But you have taken all the trouble. The motion was adopted.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.
On the recommendation of the Finance Committee, ac- counts. amonnting to £621 19s 5d were passed for pav- ment. The school fees for January amounted•to £96 16s •

WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB.

The following description of Mr. J. E. Farrell, the well- known captain of the Widnes Football team, appears in the "Football Times ar.d Cricketer's Herald " of this week, in which paper there als,r appears a photograph of Mr. Far- relit—The Widnes team may consider they have for their captain the best half-back in the South-W.est Lancashire division, who will compare favourably with those inclu- ded in a wider division, but the Chemicals have never been able to get on the right aide of the County Committee, therefora their captain has net obtained the height of am- bition fought for, and belirved by many to be fully deser- ved. 'Curly," which name he received through the nature of his hair, was born in Manchester on New 23rd, 1860, and , is therefore 25 years of age, standing sft. sin, in height, and scales 10fat. Some 20 years ago it was found necessary for Mr. Farrell, sear., to remove to Widnes to follow up his trade, in which line he soon raised up a firet-rate• business. The Subject of our sketch, growing older, was taught the same trade, and their firm, having covered nearly all the inhabitants of the district, have a standing reputation. Farrell has earned a fair share of suc- cess upon the running track, and unlike the majority of athletes, is a total abstainer from intoxicants. He com- menced his football career about nine years ago, with a now defunct Association club known as the Milton, whose cap- tain was the now renowned Lancashire covprine-point, Jack Briggs, and smother star in the team was Joe Briggs, the family haying just arrived from Nottingham, where the Association game was at that time (as now) the game prin- cipally in vogue. Farrell soon showed a preference for the handling game, and joined the Simms Cross Club, but coming under the notice of the Widnes veteran, Mr. S. H. Kenrick, he was advised to throw in his lot with the Widnes Club, where his services were soon appre- ciated, as in the twelve matches he played in during the last season he gained 19 tries. The following season, al- though not quite so succ-ssful at trv-gettieg, he showed his title to a place in the ream by kicking 16 goals in 17 attenwts. When tee Wesr-Laileashire and Border Trans Union was inaugurated, the committee recogn,z«l Farrell'e claim by selecting him to do dwy for them upon three °c- essions, the last being the nsateh against Batley, at the commencement of this seas n, in which he chained the only point gained by his side and kicked a neat goal. At the commencement of this season Farrell was unanimously elected captain of the first n am, in which capacity he has fully realized the expectations of his electors, being a great. favourite with the players and general public, and Widnes players are still hoping the time will come whea Farrell's merits will gain him a place in the bigger matches.

WARRINGTON MUSEUM AND LIBRARY. DESCRIPTION OF THE ALTERATIONS. The extensive alterations at the Museum and Public Library are now almost completed, and the re-opening of those portions of the building which have been closed during the past few months will be celebrated on Friday evening next by a conver. sazione to be gi/en by Mr. W. Beamont, the chair-. man of the Museum, Library, and Arts Committee. The alterations comprise an almost entire re-arrange- ment of the museum, library, and reading-room, and also considerable structural changes in the in- terior of the building. The visitor to the library or reading-room will now find, on entering the main doorway which opens into Bold-street, that the en- ranee to the reading-room at the opposite side of the lobby or vestibule has been the, up, and that therefore he will have to turn to the left and pass into the apartment in which before the present changes a portion of the local antiquities of the Museum were exhibited. He will then find that

this room has undergone a complete transformation. , All the Museum cases and exhibits have been re- moved, and in their places are five or six lofty double book cases, which ' -are capable of accommodating all the books which formerly, in solid array, graced three sides of the spacious read- ing-room. Besides containing these book cases this apartment had been fitted as the office of the cura- tor and his assistants. Fronting the doorway of the room is an elegant desk, surmounted with glass panels, which stretches across the room to the

-newly made entrance to the reading-room. Sh.ould the visitor wish to go into the reading-room he will pass to the right along the passage between the desk and the wall into that room, but if he be a subscriber desiring to change a book, he ,will turn. to the left, and hand his returned volume over another short counter, without the surmounting glass panels, running parallel with the Bold-street , wall of the room., in consequence of this arrange- ment the somewhat dingy looking desk and counter which formerly monopolised one end of the,reading- room have been removed, and therefore much more space is allowed to readers. The books have been removed from the shelves on two sides of the room, though the shelves themselves are still left, and thus provide an ample reserve of book-room space. At the Museum-street end of the reading-room the shelves are still.packed. with books, and here also is a counter at which books will be issued to non-subscribers. On the whole the frequenters of the reading-room are likely to be most benefited by the new arrangements. The space allotted to them is not only very largely aug- mented by the removal of the counter and desk and the rails which ran round part of the room, but their convenience is materially added to by the issu- ing department being entirely disconnected. Owing to the judicious use of glass partitions the curator and his assistants can still maintain a proper super- vision of both the library and reading-room, whilst through so many of the 'books being kept in the cases immediately behind them they will be enabled• to make; the issue much Onore conveniently and expeditiously than was _possible heretofore. Formerly the room to the right of the vestibule formed part of the Museum, but this apartment has also been divested of its specimen cases and their contents, so that the Museum is entirely ' confined to the upper floors. This room will now be used as a meeting -place for the committee, the Field Club, . and other such bodies. It ought to be mentioned also that the wall of the vestibule and stair-case are now decorated with an additional number of shields, on which are displayed the arms of notable families 'who have been more or less connected with this neighbourhood. These shields now in all number sixty-two. On ascending the stairs it will be found that the large room formerly used by the School of Art has been utilised for Museum purposes. New glass cases have been erected' round the road; and in these ere placed the specimens of vertebrate animals formerly located in the two rooms leading to the Art Gallery. The two series of British and foreign birds have consequently been. brought together in one room, a much more satis- factory arrangement both for sight-seers and ex- perts. The apartment is admirably lighted from the top, and this, together with the elegant capac- ious new cases and the excellent classification of the exhibits, makes:it one of the most attractive depart- ments of the institution. The floor of this room was formerly rather unsteady, but this defect is now remedied by the erection beneath of an iron column and girder, and as this room is immediately over the reading-room the floor has been laid with felt and linoleum to deaden the noise that may be made by visitors. It should be added that several new specimens of quadrupeds have recently been ob- tallied, but still there are several deficiencies in this. class whiCh are perhaps more obvious under, the new =augments than the old. The contents .of the two ground-floor rooms which, as we have stated have been taken upstairs, are now chiefly disposed in the two rooms which lead to the art gallery, and form a very interesting display. The- art gallery and othor portions of the Museum have ' not been much affected by the alterations, and re- main for the most part as they were, except that so far as the convenience of visitors and effective- ness of display are concerned, they have benefitted by theconcentrating process that has been carried. out. The alterations have been made from designs by Mr. W. Owen, architect, a member of the com- mittee, who has rendered his services gratuitously; and the following are the tradesmen by whom the- executive part of the work has been performed, viz.: Structural alterations and carpenters' work, Messrs. Collin and Son; book cases, Mr. Mounfleld ;. glass cases for sepcimens, &c., Messrs. IL Garnett and Sons; painting and decoration, Messrs. Hesketh and Sons. It will be agreeable to the patrons of the lending. department of the library to learn that a new cata- logue containing all the additions up to the com- mencement of the 3,ear is now in print. A glance , into its pages will show that the librarian, Mr. Madeley, in the very difficult work of compilation and arrangement has endeaveured' in every way to promote the convenience of the reader.' The cata- logue is in alphabetical order, but as far as possible [ the advantages of classification have also been secured. It has ' been said that in literature the oldest and in science the newest books are the best, and few will dispute at any rate the latter part of. this maxim. In this catalogue we find that under the subject notices the books are approximately arranged in chronological order. A. reader, for in- stance, who desires the latest information that can be had in the important science of astronomy need but turn to the subject heading "Astronomy," and then by a glance, at the bottom of the list he will see what is the latest published book on'the subject Ithat the library contains. In history a slighly dif- ferent but equally admirs.ble, and, as it were, natural, system, has been adopted. Under the head- ing of France, for example, the readerwill find that the first titles that catch his eye will be of books which treat of a large • span of the history of that country, or which , cannot foi some other reason be very easily put into chronological order, but lower down it will be seen that the order is chronological up to the most recent times. A very complete system of cross references from the great divisions of knowledge, such as the various divisions of science, history. '&c., down to almost a single book which may in any way trench upon the subject, Considering the number and variety of books that had to be ,dealt with the cata- is altogether remarkably simple and "understand- able" and is in every way a credit to the library, and to Mr. Madeley, upon whom would necessarily devolve the laborious duty of compilation and classification.

_ WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Befere Alderman Burgess. DRUNEW_NEiS.—Tht,iIIaS Higgin3 and Michael Ward were each fined 55 a.r.d oasts for this offence. I'IIEFT BY A SEUVANT.—Edward Richardson (35),unmar- tied, was charg,d. with stealing, on the 17th inst., 14ibe. of sat:sages and &be. of pork, value 12s 7d, the property of John Maddock, Pork butcher and sausage maker, 28, Wel- lingtcn-street, by whom he was employed. Prisoner, who lodges at Sankey Bridges, was sent out to deliver goods to customers and, appropriating the money, went ow the spree. It was stated that he had previously borne a good c'earac- ter, and the Bench passed sentence of 14 days' imprisonment only. ENLISTING ron e HoalE.:—George Henry Vaughan, a soldier. was charged with making a false statement on en: listm,nt at Orford Barrack. He professed never to have been in the army before,-which found to be untrue.—Pri- soner said that he had served twelve years in the army, and had always borne a good character. He made a wrong statement to enable him to enlist, because he had no home to go to.—He was sent to prison for seven days. A PUBLICAN'S DEFENCE —John Gordan, until recently landlord of the Gun Inn, Scotland-road, was charged with being drunk on the night of the 13th inst.—P.C. 37 stated that at 11-45 on the night named he WitS called to the Gun Inn, and saw defendant, who was very drunk, standing out- side his door. Defendant said "I am looking for a police- man to turn these people out," and in anewer to the con- stable's query why they were there after cleeing time, he replied that he could not get them away. The policeman, on going into the house, found there five men and three , women, and in the back yard he found two soldiers and al woman of tad character.—Defendent said that after the house had iieen closed his wife found some Men hiding in. the cellar, and he, being afraid to turn them out unaidFd, called some men from the street to assist him. He denied being drunk.—lt was stated that defendant's license ex- pired that dey. He was fined 55 and costs. Misnzetessous. Mary Ann Holmes, widow, no fixed residence, was charged with drunkenness ; she was dis- missed with a cant-loc.—Patrick Quinn (14), described by Inspector Berry as an "intolerable nuisance" was sent to prison for seven days for sleeping out in the stable of the Patten Arms Hotel.—Margaret O'Brien, for being drunk and disordely on Town Hill on the 16th inst, was fined 103 or 14 days' imprisonment, and Annie McGuire, for a simi- lar offence committed in Berry's-yard on the 14th inst, was fined 5s and costs.—,-Margaret • Fleming (30th appearance), and Catherine Carey, were charged with fighting in Horse- market en the 16th inst, and were ordered each to find a surety for their future good bahaviour.—Catherine Troy was fined for keeling lodgers without having her house re- gistered, and a eimi-ear charge against Michael Grime. was adjourned.
GOOD TEMPLA.RISM IN. SoUTII-WEST
LANCASHIRE.

The annual session of the South-West Lancashire District Lodge of Good Templars was held in the rooms of the Young Men's Christian Association, Mount Pleasant, Liverpool, on Monday evening,when there was a large attendance of lodge delegates, in- cluding rethers J W Hall, J Price, and J Sheath, Warrington ; J Bird, St. Helens; John Thompson and Charles Webb, Wianes; George Clarke and John Taylor, Earlestown. Brother R W presided. After the roll call and other formal busi- ness the annual reports were submitted. The W.D. Sec. (Brother R W Kirkus) showed the numerical position of the order to be over 2900 inembers, a slight decrease in comparison with the previous year; the W.D. Treasurer gave a very favourable report, show- ing a balance in hand, after paying all expenses and a deficiency from list year; the report of the Execu- tive alluded to the conferences and united gatherings during the year ; and the District Electoral Superintendent (Brother M Jones) reported that an active electoral work was 2arried on , and especially at the time of the general eleetiou. , The District Superintendent of Juvenile Temples (Bro. B. Preston) reported that there were 29 Temples I with 2.065 members, an increase of two Temples and 150 memlwre. The election of officers for the ensuinie year afterwards took place, and amongst those elected were the following ;—District Chief Templar, Bro. J W. Hall, Warrington ; D.V.T., Sister E, Porter, Liverpool ; D. Councillor, Bro. George Clarke, Earlestown; D. Secretary, Bro. M. Jones, Liverpool; D. Treasurer, Bro. J. J. Wright, Liverpool: D.SJ.T. Bro. R Ander,, Liverpool ; D. Sentinel, Bro. J. Bird, St Helens; and District Electoral Superintendent, Brother J. Rekeisgill, Liverpool. Hearty thanks were accorded to the officers for their services during the past year, and it was decided that the next quar- terly session should be held at Earlestown. The fol- lowing were elected to represent the District Lodge at the General Lodge Session, at Newport, South Wales :—Sisters Green and Collings (Liverpool), Brothers J. W. Hall (Warrington), G. Clarke (Earles- town), Williams and Kirkus (Liverpool), and P. J. Whitehead (Southport.) The session was one of the most interesting for some considerable time.

Inquiries were consequently made, and it appeared that a matt named " John " bad left the articles at Mrs. Riley's house, and had .since left the town. A ERINSER.—Edwin Cooke, a young man, on the evi- dence of P,C. Millington was convicted of fighting in Fryer- street on the 4th met, and was bound over to keep the peace for six months in his own recognizances of £5. ASSAI7LT.—Mary Shallcross was charged with assaulting Mary Haman, a married woman, living in Duke-street. It was alleged that on the 15th February the defendant accused the complainant of keeping a bad house and struck her on the forehead with her fist.—Defendant said there was danc- ing and singing going on in the complainant's until two and three o'clock every Monday morning, and her children could not sleep. She denied striking the complainant. She only shoved her. A fine of 5s and costs, us 6d, was imposed. OBSTETCTING THE FOOTPLTII—George Pye, a youth who lives in Lord-street, was charged with obstructing the foot- path. P.S. Neild said on Sunday night, the 7th inst, he saw the defendant throw a "War Cry" over a young woman's head in Bridge-street. He then commenced to wrestle with her on the footpath and-caused an obstruction. Fined Is and costs, Os 6d. VAGRANTS.—John McDonald, an old man, who was re- leased from gaol on Saturday, was again charged with begging on that day. P.C. Ember proved the case. The prisoner had is lid and a large quantity of bread in his possession and was very drunk. He was sentenced to 21 days' hard lebonr.—On the evidence of P.C. Wallace, Wm. Dales' was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour for begging in Greenwa-e-road on Sunday.—John Evans and James Dillon, respectable-looking men, were charged with begging in Bridge-street. Evave had na and Dillon is 5d in copper. Evidence was given by P.C. Wallace. Evans was sent to gaol for seven days and Dillon was discharged. A WILD Youru.—Walter Kinsey, 14 years of age, was brought up for remand charged with sleeping on a bo'at in the Bridgewater Canal.—The father appeared, and said he could do no good with the lad, who had only slept at home four or five times during so many weeks.—Superintendent Leah said the boy had a good home.—The boy was dis- charged orvpromising to improve his ways, and the father was advised to send him to sea.

• It is reported that the men who have been on strike owing to a wages dispute at the Llanberis quarries will re- sume work next week, having accepted the employers' terms. The strike has lasted 19 weeks. A PRESTON PUBLICAN SCALDED TO DEATH—On Wednes- day evening a Preston publican, named John Pilkington, died at his house from the effects of terrible injuries he re- ceived in the morning. The deceased was brewing, and his wife, hearing screams she ran into the brew-house and found he had fallen into a large mash tub full of boiling water. She got him out at once. He was fearfully scalded. Dr. Wamsley was sent for, bat the man rapidly grew worse and expired. Btu-IAL REFORM. —On Thursday morning, in both Houses ot the Northern Convocation, petitions were pre- sented by the Bishop of Soder and Man and Archdeacon Hamilton advocating a return te the simplicity of burial advocated in the Order for the Burial of the Dead, namely, burial in pnishable coffins in mother earth, a method which' obsJrves the well-defined laws of nature, avoids sanitary evils, and leaves the earth ready for the next generation to exercise its heneficient actions again. THE LONDON RIOTS.—TRE OFFICIAL INQUIRY.—Th report was issued on Tuesday of the special committee ap- pointed to inquire into the arrangements made by the Lon- don police to meet contingencies that might arise out of the recent meetings, at the close of which rioting took place. After an exhaustive review of the evidence and the facts, the committeearrived at the conclusion that the police rangements for the meeting were most unsatisfactory and very defective in their.conception. The force provided eras Insufficient, and the Chief Commissioner's instructions were too meagre in 'character and did not provide for contineen- cies which the police ought to have foreseen. The great fault committed during, the day was that no arrangements were made for controlling the action of the mob after it had broken up, although it was well understood that a large ele- mentof a very dangerous clasS was present. It was a serious mistake for the officer in command on such an oc- cagion to be in plain clothes, which made it quite impossible for him to exercise any effective command. It was also a great mistake that no.monnted police were employed. The ownmittee are atrongly of opinion that bad the police authoritieS shown greater resource in acting upon a good and well . tindirstood system the mob might have been effectively headed and easily broken up at an early period of their progress Havirig pointed out what titries them as most conspicuous in the faultiness of the pohce arrange- ments, the committee call attention to the most urgently reqiiired reforms in the police system. spector Greenwell, an officer of the R.S.P.Q.A., stationed at 1 Altrincham, prosecuted. It appeared from the evidence that the defendant, who was in the employ of Mr. Leach, had applied paraffin oil to the inside of the pony's leg and then set the oil OR fire. The result was that the animal's skin had been much burnt, and for three weeks it had been unable to leave the stable. Defendant said he had done this in order to burn off the long hairs so that the horse might look "as nice as any other body's horse."—A fine of 5s and costs was imposed. STEALING CAELIFLOWERS.—MichaeI Griffin, a labourer, was chargeo on a warrant with having stolen from a field in Latchford three cauliflowers, value Ot, the property of Wil- iam Lamb. M. Lamb said be had Ire9uently missed cauliflowersifrom the field in question, and setting watch he saw the prisoncr cut and carry three away. Prisoner said he went to see if the cauliflowers were damaged, and find- ing they were damaged he took three.—A fine of lOs and costs wae imposed, or in default ,14 days' imprison- ment. A FnlvoLors CASE.—Thomas Parsonage Taylor and Wil- liam Ticket, farmers, Preston Brook, were charged with having on the 2nd January trespassed in search of conies on land belon7ing to a neighbouring farmer named William Turner Brereton. Mr. Fox (from Messrs. R. Davies and Co's. office, Warrineton). appeared for the complainant, and Mr. A. Browne for the defendants. Mr. Brereton said he was the occupier of the Windmill Farm, Preston Brook. He bad the right of taking the game on the farm, but he never gave the clefendants permission to go on his land. In answer to Mr. Browne, witness said Mr. Tickle's land ad- joined his own. Formerly Mr. Tickle and he were ver-y friendly. Taylor was still a tenant of his, and as yet they had had no disputes about improvements. The summonses were not ieeeed out of spite. John Robinson, Thomas Rob- inson, and Arnold Platt, labourers in the employ of the complainant, spoke to having seen the defendants on the hatter's land, one of them having a Lrret and the other a gnu. For the defence it was contended that Mr. Taylor and Mr. Tickle were .really in search of a ferret which had been lost on the pre7ious day. The Chairman said that was a frivoloue case and it was a pity to find that neighbours could not agree. The qaestion was so very small a one that the Bench would only impose a penalty of is and costs on each defendant.

RUGBY RULES. WAIIRINGTO!.7 ROVERS V. TRANMEBE IS-T.—The above match was played on Saturday, on the ground of the former, and, after a hard and pleasant game, resulted in a victory fur the visitors by two tries and three minor points to three minor points. The tries were both obtained by M. Court. Teams :—Tranrnere : Full back, Whyte; tbree-quarter backs Blundell, Fulton, and Pickford ; half-backs, M. Court and G. Court • forwards, Dr. Crellin, Short, Williams, Collins, Hopkins, Nicholls, Lees, Watson, and Edwards. Revers: Full hack, Alton; throe-quarter backs, Randles' W. Bellian, and Allen ; half-backs, Fair (captain) and G.Bellian ; for- wards, Hackett, Mclntyre, Webster, Roberts, Grahame, Mather, Denham, Barlow, and Savage. Umpires, J. Hux- ham and W. Brown. Referee, R. Sudlow. WIDNES V. Sr. CLEMENTS (ROCEIDALE.)7—ThefIe teams met on the Widnes ground on Saturday, one of the best matches of the season being the result. The visiting team played a grand combined game, and the Widnes forwards evidently met their equals. In the first half Widnes were compelled to touchdown upon two occasions, and it was not until late in the second halt that Pennington was enabled to get a try, through some good passing in which Ridyard, S. Bingham, and Farrell had a hand. Widnes played a good defensive game, the backs tackling in fine style, particularly Ridyard, who was never seen to better advantage. The Widnes team was as follows : F. Plumpton, back ; R. Pennington, Bingham, and S. Morris, three quarters; T. Ridyard and E Farrell, half backs • J. Goulden, J. Gandy, J. Hardman, J. Petvin, P. Corns, T. Fogg, J. A. Brown, J. Bingham, and W. Meagher, forwards. RUNCORN OLD BOYS (IST) V. FAENNVORTH —This return fixture was carried out on Saturday afternoon on the Old Buys' ground, and after a hard-fought game the home team caine oil victorious, notwithstaniing that some of their best players were absent. At half-time the visitors had scored one try and three minor points to the Old Bays one minor. On resuming play, however, the boys had things much their own way, they scoring one goal;one disputed try, and three other minor points, whilst Farnworth were unable.to add. any additional point. Amongst those of the home team who played s_pe.cially well as forwards may be mentioned Higgins, We's, Timpertey, Prince, and Jones. D. Knight (capt.) and Robinson at half-back acquitted themselves creditably, as did also Abram!, and Griffiths at three-quarter. I The play of Dobson at foil back was characterized by cool-

ness and precision. All the visitors' backs played very well, but their forwards did not evince the systematic play that was manifested by their opponents. For the home team the try (which resulted in a goal, nicely kicked by Higgins) was securcd by Abrams, immodiately after it had

, been well taken to the opponents' 25 by one of the irresistible rushes that so inarllNl the play of the 011 Boys. and in which D. Knight was seen doing some good 'dribbling. RUNCORN V. LIVERPOOL GYMNA SlUM—There is gener-
ally,a large amount of local interest taken in the meeting of these teatns, and the encounter of Saturday was no ex-

ception to the ml", a large crowd of spectators witnessing a (pick ;atne, which was won isy the Runcorn men by one .1 goal, four tries, three minor points, to one minor point. The , individual play of the home team was capital. In the back division Wools played-a very safe game, clearing his lines very effectually. The three-quarter backs played well, Lunt and Jehnson making strong efforts repeatedly to score. Speakman was in his nsual!y good form his tries (two) be- ing the reeult of sterling play. B. Hughes and H, Andrews (half hacks) played a god game throughout. Of the for- wrrds, Joule Was to the fore in some fine dribbles. Barns, Dean, Broady, and Hughes showed frequently in loose for- ward play. In the visitors' team the full back, Stacey. played a capital full back game, returning the ball well out .of danger. Edwards was the most prominent of the three- quarter backs, Bailey ably supporting him. Butcher at half back did a lot of work, collaricg well, and putting in some excellent runs. The forwarcla played a fairly good game, 1 Monteith, Dufton, Roberts, and Williams being the most prominent in the pack. The tries were obtained by Speak- man (two), Wainwright, H. Hughes, and Dant, the latter putting in some brilliant runs. Teams :—Runcorn: Woods, back; Lunt, Johnson, and Speakman, three•quarter backs; H. Hughes and Andrews, half backs; Broady, Hughes. Lewis, Joule, Dean, Barns,Gatley, Clarke, and Wainwright, forwards. Gymnasium : Stacey, back; Bailey, Hall, and Edwards, three-quarter backs; Smith and Butcher, half backs; Trevitt, Roberts, Monteath, Williams, Dawn, Keay, Gunson, Leek, and Sylvester, forwards. WARRINGTON v. ASRTON-L'NDER-LYNE.—The return match between these two teams was played at Ashton, on Saturday last, in beautiful weather, and in the presence of 1,500 spectators._ The visitors were without the services of

Warren, Fairfield Turner, Torn Barnes, and lUgby, and it was thought by many that they were in for a sound thrash- ing, but contrary to expectation they scored a very decisive victory by two tries to one minor, after a very well-fought game. Play commenced by F. Turner kicking eff for War- rington, and after exchange of kicks between Warren and Massey the first scrimmage was formed in the centre. Ashton next rushed the ball up to the visitors' 25, where was fought some well-contested scrimmages. Massey relieving for a short time, but eventually the oval was brought back again, Catterall taking a drop at goal, a touchdown resulting. Warrington now seemed to settle down to their work, for by grand combined play the ball was taken with a rush to the home 25. Next ensued a lot of give and take play, Hewitt and Garside on one siet.e, and Buxton and Massey on the other, relieving the monotony by short runs. Gilbert was next to the front by a good run, and transferring to Massey, this play gained ground by kicking into touch. Catterall now obtained possession, but was well stopped by Speakman before getting dangerous. From a loose scrimmage Hough got hold, and on being collared passed to Dillon, this player by a grand effort scoring the first try, Buxton failing at the place. After another exchange of kicks between the backs, Gilbert got in a smart run, and passing very neatly to Speakman, the latter player, overcoming all oppositipn, grounded the oval over the line, Jolley this time being en- trusted with the place but failed to convert it into a major point. Half time, with the ball in the centre of the field, was shortly afterwards called. On resuming, Frank Turner and Gilbert led ciff with a grand dribble to the home 25, the ball remaining here for some time. In this half nothing was scored, Massey and Speakman playing extremely well, and Jolley putting in some dashing runs. Time being called brought to an end a pleasantly-contested game. Hewitt at back was quite up to form, the three-quarters and halves played a grand combined game, and as for the forwards, we are at a loss to distinguish the pick. Davies, Hough, Dillon, and Ashton were perhaps the most prominent. Warren and Catterall played well for the home team. Povey, Ashton, Nevins, and Hough also got over, but the trries were not allowed. Teams :—Warrington : Back, Hewitt; three- quarters. Jolley, Buxton, and Massey; half-backa, Gilbert and Speakman; forwards, Dillon Povey, Littlewood, Nevins, Heyes, Frank Turner, Davies, dough, and Ashton. Ashton: Back, Warren ; three-quarters, Garside (captain), Catterall, and Smith; half-backs, Lawton and Heap; forwards; Brown. Fitton, Johnson, Hamer' Hawley. Hague, Walsh, White- head, and Williamson. Referee, J. Briggs, Manchester.

• ASSOCIATION RULES. WIGAN DISTRICT .CUP.—SEMI-FINAL. GOLBORNE V. HINDLEY.—This match was played at Wigan, on Saturday, before 2,500 spectators. Play was very fast and even, the result at half-time being one each. Amidst excitement each goal was attacked alternately. Golborne shot through, but the point was disallowed for off-side, nod bad the best of play towards the finish, but failed to win. The result , was a tie—one each. LIVERPOOL CUP TIE: BARLESTOWN V. STANLEY (LIVERPOOL). ••• The meeting of these clubs at Earlestown on Saturday afternoon to decide their tie in the fourth round of the com- petition for the Liverpool and District Challenge Cup ex- cited an unprecedented interest throughout the district. As there was no other match in the neighbourhood, the attend- ance of spectators was very large. Considerably over 1,000 persons assembled, notwithstanding the threatening char- acter of the weather. They were rewarded by witnessing one of the best and most evenly fought contests of the season, the result at the finish being declared a draw, each :ide having scored one goal. The visitors were represented by their possible strongest team, while, unfortunately for the Earlestenians, the latter were unable to have the ser- vices of their captain, A. W. Dagnall, who had not re- covered from the injury to his knee received in the match against Blackburn Park Road on the previous Saturday. From the commencement excitement ran very high—the visitorls having been accompanied by a large number of their supporters from Liverpool. Macgregor set the leather in motion up the hill, and Stanley immediately assumed the aggressive, and the belt went over the line. Sims ran down his win, from the goal kick, but a good return by Dick enabled Smith to get well up, and he was only foiled by R. Green at the expense of a corner, which Pollock placed be- hind. Each goal was afterwards visited in rapid succession. and Brown, after a good run, was just steadying himself fur a final shot when R. Green upset his calculations, awl the ball went wide. Culkin then troubled Appleton, who threw the ball away, Macgregor returning it along the ground, but again he cleared his lines by a good kick. Bowker and Duxbury were conspicuons for some fine play in midfield, and, working the baell well down, a fierce scrimmage took place in front of the Stanley citadel, and a loud cheer and waving of bats announced its downfall from the foot of Siddelay. Appleton saved a bet one from Macgregor, and after a visit to the end by Rich, who was robbed by Kerr, the Stanley forwards came again, and Appleton fisted out from Smith. Culkin met the return and passed to Mac- gregor, who had the ball through, but was ruled off-side, and half time arrived. Ends were then changed, and tht, gems recommenced amid renewed excitement. Three minutes after the resumption Wilson enabled Macgregor Ca equalise the score with a low shot, Rich and Ellison re- turned to the attack, and a shot from the former caused Wright to handle, which he did in a clever style. The ball was again down in Earlestown quarters, and Smith kicked into Appleton's bands, and immediately afterwards Sims made a good attempt at the other erd, rut the ball went a yard wide, although some of the distant spectators thought B rAiswi ca Brown nt timee r nu were drewneirneoa f encouraged ot tickler,hae c 81 Psaceut, ad andtolbYrysr the afisloedalohuatdonbeufnrosmcoSreidm.s. be- camese score intense. remained Teghuea thea; les toe enthusiastic shouts of their spectators, and during the last five minutes they made desp:rate efforts to secure a leading po'nt. DEPRESSED TRADE COMMISSION.—The meeting of the Royal Commission on Depression of Trade was held at Whitehall, on Thursday, Lord Iddesleigh presiding. Mr. Jacob Behrens, of Bradford, was examined as to the condi- tion of the woollen industry, and on Thursday afternoon some witnesses from Belfast gave evidence as to the condi- dition of the lines trade. ALLEGED MURDER AT HULL.—On Wednesday morning woman named Louisa Wharan, who was divorced from her husband, was found in a house in Edward Place, Hull, with her head almost severed from the body. It reas first thought she had committed suicide, but circumstances afterwards transpiring leading to the suSpicion that she had been mur- dered. A man named W. Corp, with whom she had been keeping company, was. arrested, and on Wednesday arter- noon was formally charged by the police with wilful murder. In a statement made to the nonce, Corp said be awoke a few minutes after seven, and saw the deceased cutting her throat with a knife.. He knocked it out of la,r band, but she got up, seized another knife, and commenced hack- ing her throat. He then raisefi an alarm and went for a policeman.
(Indian Blood Purative.)

- THE SUPPOSED MIT.RDER OF A POLICEMAN IN WAR- WICXSHIRE.—BIoodhounds were used on Saturday its the hope of being able to trace the body of the policeman Hine. Several detectives and constables of the Warwickshire police directed the search for the missing man. A short time ago en attempt was made by poachers to mnrder him, but they were prevented by the arrival of timely assistance. The police have succeeded in finding a knife with blood stains upon it close to the spot where evidences of a strug- gle were seen on the g.iound. The weapon is an ordinary Pocket-knife, and it was found in a ditch beneath a thick hedge. On Wednesday afternoon the body itself was found.. The police who had been dragging the cmal at Fenny Compton for the missing constable, found the body within a short distance of the public-house where the officer was last seen. There was a wound in the neck which seems to have been caused by a knife, and behind th 3 left ear was another wound, apparently inflicted by some blunt inatza- ment.

THE TRIAL @l' SOCIALISTS.—The examination at Bow- strest of Messrs. Burns, Hyndtnan, Champion, and Williams for seditious speech was proceeded with on Wednesday. Sir James Ingham declined to interfere in respect to certqn publications reflecting on the case, as he said the defendants bad a remedy at law. Mr. Barling, of the Daily Telegraph, was recalled, and said in cross-examination he did not see either Burns or Williams in Pall Mall or St. james's-street. Neither did he see any police. He had never is his ex- p?rience soon such a remarkable absence of mile° all iha way. In Hyde Park Williams and Burns asked the crowd to disperse in an orderly manner. He could not say if his original notes had been destroyed or thrown away. Edgar Windset, a cricket-bat maker, said he saw Burns wave a red flag at the base of Nelson's Column. All the defendants were there. Mr. Chamberlain was placed in the witness box, on the application of the defendants, and depcsed the deputation waiting on him the day after the riots, but he did not se them. Ho read the correspondence which has been published. There was, be said, no , doubt that the distress in the country was severe and exceptional. The defendants were remanded until Saturday. div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The international match between Scotland and Ireland at Edinburgh resulted in the total detest of the Irish team by four goals and two tries to nothing. Bradford and Manchester met on the ground of the for- mer, before 8,000 spectators, who were treated to a grand game of footall, which ended in a victory for Bradford by one goal, three tries, and six minor points, to nil. Dewsbury sent a very poor team to oppose Salford, the consequence being the total defeat of the Yorkshirernen by two goals and two tries to nil. Swinton are evidently showing better form as the season advances, for on Saturday, after journeying to Bat- ley, they managed to beet the cupholders by one goal and one try to one goal, the minors being equal. Oldham received a visit from Broughton Bangers, who had to retire beaten by one goal and three minors to one try and Gne minor. The Rangers were without four of their I best men.

That was a crushing defeat which Birkenhead Park re- ceived at the hands of the Broughton Club, which was played on the ground of the latter, the score being at call of time Broughton three goals and five tries to Birkenhead Park two tries.
One of the finest games seen on the Widnes ground was between ti+e Widnes club and Rochdale St. Clements, which resulted in a win for the chemicals by one try to a couple of minors.
Warrington went as far as Ashton to play off their return fixture, and though they bad four of their bast men away they managed to defeat the Ashton team by a couple of tries to a brace of minors
Liverpool Gymnasium went as far as Runcorn, but the home team were too good, winning easily by one goal, four tries and three minors, to one minor.

St. Helens are looking up, having defeated Cherlton by one try. One of the most nteresting of Saturday's fixtures was the cup tie at Earlestown between Stanley and the present holders of the local trophy. The LiVerpool team was in full force, and with a strong forward contingent, made matters very warm for the home defenders. The constitution of the attacking part:;, was perfectly remodellei, consisting of J. Wilson and Smith on the right, MtGregor centre, and Brows and Cu!kin on the left. It will be seen that there no longer exists here the lightness which has proved so serious a handicapping in the previous matches of Stanley. The match at Earlestown is characterised as "hard," free from unpleasant incidents for such an exciting affair, and ended in a draw of one goal each. Earlestown had not the sr- vices of their captain, Dagnali, who was irjured at Black- burn, and when they scored the first goal the greatest en- thusiasm was manifested. Anxiety succeeded when McGregor put the teams on an equality, and this feeling was predominant for the rest of the watch, which resulted in a drawn game. The tie will now 13? played off at Walton- stiles next Saturday, when Stanley should just win. It will be a very hard game, however. Runcorn had a visit from Liverpool Gymnasium, and a . _
good fast game ensued, the Gym suffering defett to the tune of 1 coal and 4 tries to a minor point. Speakman (2), Hughes, Lunt, and Wainwright were the scorers, but they

, .. _ were ably supported by Joull, Bares, and Hughes in the pack, Woods and Johnson playing finely behind. For the Gym. Edwards, Bailey, and Stacey behind, Monteath, Daf- t" and Willi.crts played very bard forward. _ _

The Conference of International Football Associationists was held on Tuesday at the North-Western Hotel, Liver- pool. England would not agree to the agenda paper put forward, and was not represented; but the other three por- tions of the kingdom were—Messrs. M‘Killop and Brown appearing- for Scotland, Messrs. Sinclair and Hanna for Ire- land, and Messrs. Hunter and Taylor for Wales. The fol- lowing resolutions were passed unanimously, and will be submitted to the English Association :-1. That each Na- tional Association shall define for itself what it considers a professional. 2. That a professional of one country shall rank as a professional in the others, and the same with amateurs. 3. Clubs of one country shall not play against professionals of the same nationality who play for clubs of another country, unless they (the professionals) have been resident three years; but clubs of the same country may play against each other without this restriction. Residenci to have the meaning dc..fined by the English Association 4. Qualification for an international player to be birth in the country for which be plays; inter-country and inter-associ- ation snatches to come un(ter Resolution 3. 5 That a con- ference of the four National Associations be held annagy in June, to be called by each in turn. A meeting of the committee of the Lancashire Football Association was held at Darwen on Monday evening. The coacimittee suspended for the rest of the season a player named Abel Heys, employed by the Everton Football Club, in consequence of his having violated the professional rules by playing for more than one club in a season without the consent of the Football Association. A team was then chosen to represent the Lancashire Juniors against Northumberland, on the Woodside Ground, Bolton, on Saturday.

div.head: SHIP CANAL BILL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL BILL.

A correspondent says :—Mr. Houldsworth has taken charge of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill in the House of Commons, and will move the second reading. The return for which Mr. Craig Sellar moved, showing the time occu- pied and the expense incurred in the promotion of the Man- chester Ship Canal Bill in the past three sessions, has just been laid on the table of the House, and it will be printed in the usual course. It is intended to be used by the hon. gentleman as an argument in favour of the amendment of the present costly system of private bill DEPUTATION TO MR. MUNDELLA.

On Tuesday the promoters of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill and several Lancashire and Cheshire members of Par- , liamen,t had an interview with Mr. Mundella, at the Board of Trade, to urge the Government to support the second reading of the bill, which is threatened with opposition from the railway companies of the district. Mr. HOULDSIVORTH, M.P., having recapitulated the his- tory of the scheme, said the bill now before Parliament was one to enable the Manchester Ship Canal Company to pay interest on capital during construction. It proposed to pay interest to the shareholders on the amount from time to time paid up on the shares, at a rate of interest not exceeding 4 per cent., the interest only to be paid for the time authe- rized by the companies Act for the completion of the works, or a less time if the directors determined, but not to be pay- able until the company has obtained a Board of Trade cer- tificate to the effect that two-thirds of the capital has been issued, the interest not to accrue upon any shares on which any call is in arrear ; the amount to be paid for interest not to exceed £752,000; and the bon owing powers of the company to be reduced by one-fourth of the sum paid in interest; such reduction to be made for the last instal- ment of £500.000 authorized by the Act to be borrowed; every prospectus of the company, and every certificate ois shares, to contain a notice that the company has the power ' so to pay interest; and, finally, the half-yearly accoants of the company are to show the amount of capital on which and the rate at which such interest or dividend had been paid. Under the present system the law lent itself very much to evasions, and he believed the practical effect was this, that while the very kind of companies which no doubt the Legis- lature intended to preclude, viz., promoters' companies, contractors' companies, bogus companies of all kinds, were able to evade this provision of the Legislature, bona fide companies which came straight to Parliament had this bar In their way. A great deal might be said against the prin- ciple that Parliament had apparently set up, but Parliament had not condemned the practice of paying interest out of capital absolutely. In 1882 the House of Commons relaxed the standing orders as regarded railways so far as to allow those powers to be put into an Act of Parliament, it they saw well to pass them. They did not believe, though Lord Itedeslale had held 'otherwise, that the standing orders of Parliament on payment of interest out of capital applied to an undertaking of this kind. It only applied to railways. But if it did, Parliament had waived the objection in the case of the Regent Railway and Canal Bill last year, and the House of Commons' standing orders now left it to the Select Committee to say whether interest should be paid out of capital during construction. All the great railways constructed previous to 1843 had the power now sought for by the promoters of the bill. This was a large undertaking, requiring ten millions sterling, and the time for construc- tion was put down in the bill at seven years, but they ex- pected to complete it in four years. This was an undertak- ing which could not be opened in sections, like a railway, and there could be no chance of making any profit, and this was not a time for capitalists to lie out of interest. If the bill passed, it was an absolute certainty that they would get the capital that they required. The MAYOR of MANCHESTER spoke of the great impetus to trade that the canal would give to the district. He was sure that unless Parliament allowed interest to be paid oat of capital, the Ship Canal would not be made. Mr. Alderman HUSBAND (of Salford) urged that Salford regarded this new water way as an absolute necessity for communication between Manchester and Liverpool and the rest of the world. Mr. MUNDF,LLA asked why this clause for payment of in- terest out of capital was not insisted upon. Mr. Cokries said if they had it would have been fatal to the bill, as opposition was threatened, and they only had their bill passad a few days before Parliament rose. Mr. AGNEW, M.P., said the average investor was well able to take care of himself, and that was really the whole crux of the matter. If the Government would give the imprima- tur of their sanction to this bill, they would receive the warmest' thanks of hundreds of thousands of people. , Sir JAMES FERGuSSON, M.P., said be had been recently in Bristol. and they were talking of a canal from Bristol to Birmingham, by altering and improving the existing canals, and it would not be necessary to go to Parliament. They would have the privilege of paying interest during construc- tion, whilst the Manchesler Canal might be restrained. Sir Henry Roscoe, M.P., Mr. Platt (Oldham), Mr. Bates (of the Wholesale Co-operative Society of Lancashire), and Mr. Marshall Stevens having spoken in support of the Bill,

THE GIANT. A crafty old soul is the Giant Drink! He sits by the great highway,. And watche4the numerous passengers Who traverse it day by day; Some who are revelling in Life's bright morn, When Youth tinges all things with gold, And some who have lived through the noon-tide of

life, And now have grown weary and old. The Giant, he sees them passing by. And lustily shouteth he : "Come hither! come hither! my right good friends, And rest awhile with me! Yo are wearied and thirsty, then step aside, And quaff this ruddy wine; I have brought it for you from the vineyards fair That look on the lovely Rhine. "Come hither! come hither! I'll give you health, And vigour in every limb; And the eyes shall sparkle with laughing mirth, That now with tears are dim; I will drive away, with my magic wand, The cares that rack your brain, I will cheer the sad, I will make them glad, I will soothe the sufferer's pain !" • And some there are 'mid the passers-by , Who list to the Giant's voice, And turn aside from the great highway To drink his nectar choice; Some are young men, and others are old; Some of them)seek relief That cannot be found in the maddening cup, From sickness, from anguish, from grief. And some are women—maidens.and wives— Women, who ought to be Like the mariners' beacons that radiance shed Far over the boundless sea, Guiding the sailor through darkness and storm, And pitiless, blinding blast, To the longed-for haven, where Peace spreads her wings, And danger and trial are past. Oh! a crafty soul is the Giant Drink! And he laughs a cunning iaugh When he sees his victims, young and old, From his sparkling goblet quaff; And around tnem all he casts his chains, And bears them off in glee, As slaves, fettered and bound, to spend their lives In his Castle of Misery. Young man' have a care, and maiden beware, For still by the groat highway Sits the Giant Drink, and he watches you Who traverse it day by day. Oh! heed not his calls, but pass him by, Though wearied thou mayst be; Seek not to rest in his gilded hall, Drink not what he offers thee. Oh! touch not the cup of ruddy wine, For an adder lurketh there, Ready to dart at the lips that taste, Beware of its sting, beware! Go,tpray to thy God that the time may come When the Temperance flag shall wave O'er a sober people, whom Giant Drink Shall never more enslave! Preston, Feb. 17th, 1886. EXCELSIOR.
TarietitO.

There is often room for much courage in speech courage not so much to maintain opinions as to con- fess ignorance. An insolvent actor made a statement of his indebted- ness, and, with the ruling spirit strong in bankruptcy, he added, "For 'further particulars see small bills." Visitor to a show, to the little girl who takes the cash: "We have made a bet, and we want you to settle it. Is the bearded lady your mother or your aunt ? " Little girl: "She is my father." A Scotch farmer's son was one evening visiting his sweetheart; when a violent storm came on. He rose at once to take his leave, as he said he would require to see to the safety of his father's sheep. At this his lady-love, getting between him and the door, said, "I canna let you oot in sic a nicht. They can look after the rest o' yer faither's sheep who likes, but I'll tak' care o' ane o' them." The true art of moral culture is to balance extravagant tendencies by quickening those which are languid. Growth is a safer means of producing harmony in charac- ter than repression. You cannot descend to the regions of' the lower nature and wrestle with success there.. You must go above, and fight evil inclinations, as Perseus fought the dragon that would have destroyed Andromeda, on wings in the air. . Two tramps, one of them a young man, the other well advanced in life, had just:left a house where they had been supplied with a bountiful dinner. "I say, Bill," queried the younger of the two, "where do you s'pose we'll get our supper?" The old tramp turned on him in disgust. "Here—you've just had your dinner," he said, "and you begin to wonder where you'll• get supper! If that's the kind of disposition you've got, young feller, you had better quit the profession and go to wor14!" THE WHIT], ROSH OE SCOTLAND.—This :was for many years the house of Lady Mary Clerk, of Pennicuick, known as "The White Rose of Scotland." This lady; whose maiden name was Dacre, was the daughter of -6 gentleman in Cumberland, and came into the world in that memorable year when the Highland Army was in possession of Carlisle. While her mother was still con., fined to bed, a Highland party, under a chieftain of the Macdonald clan, came to her house, but the commander, on learning the circumstances, not only chivalrously restrained his men from levying 'any ;contribution, but took from his bonnet his own white rose or cockade, and pinned it on the infant's breast, "that it might protect the household from any trouble by others. This rosette the lady kept to her dying day." lii after years she be- i came the wife of Sir James Clerk. of Pennicuick, Bart., and from time to time, on special occasions, always wore this white rose of the house of Stuart.—Frays " Cassell's Odd and New Edinburgh." A PATRIOTIC DO.—The mother of Belle, by the way, is the Most intelligent living dog that I know. She sets an example to the whole household, inasmuch as she not only opens the door of her master's study, but turns round and shuts it when she has entered the room. With this she has marked political views, refusing scraps when told that they come from certain statesmen, though she gets confused, it must be admitted, among the lesser lights. Her patriotiam, however, is never shaken. Her master has only to say' "Lass, what are you prepared to do for your country ?' and in a moment sne is a stiffened corpse on her back, her four legs sticking out like those of a stool. Of course she can when desired, point suc- cessivelaiwitii het naae to, and sometimes tutu over, all the court cards in a pack spread on the ground. But that is easily accounted for. A piece of bread-and-butter is laid under each during the earlier lessons in and re- hearsals of the performance; and the recollection of the agreeable discovery following this dainty " deal" is not i soon forgotten. It s worth while exploring every court card on the chance of a bite, when a pack appears on the ground.—Rev. Harry Jones in Leisure Hour." AN IMMENSE GRANITE SLAB.—It is no easy task to separate from the main ledge a slab of granite 354 feet long, 3 to 4 feet thick, and 11 feet wide. But this, it appears, has been accomplished at the Flynt Granite Quarries, Monson, Massachusetts, and by the means usual in all quarries for separating slabs or blocks from the main ledge. A row of wedges were set, several hun- dred in number, and the workmen, beginning at one end, gently and carefully tapped the wedges, moving by de- grees dawn the line until the other end of them was reached, when the same operation was repeated. In this manner, by careful and patient application, aided by favourable conditions of the weather, the slab of the above phenomenal size was successfully separated from ! the main rock.
