ILife is at best but a question of opportunity. NIGHT-THOUGLIT.—If every dog has its day, every night has its cat. Though we travel the world over to find the beautiful, we must carry it with us, or we find it not. To maintain an opinion because it is thine, and not be- cause it is true, is to prefer thyself above the truth. Many a man would like to begin the Christian life if he could begin it somewhere in the middle. If he could only turn about when nobody was looking; if when all the world were asleep or away he could slip quietly into the kingdom of God, and take his seat with the air of a man who had been seated there all the time! It is the turning over of the leaf when everybody is reading it— it is tho rightabout face on the crowded street when everybody will see the act and what it means—this it is which makes it easier to put off till to-morrow the su- preme duty which ought to be done to-day. During a recent term of the Circuit Court in Madison County, Miss., a negro witness was on the stand giving his testimony, which was somewhat roundabout and evasive. Finally the State's attorney interrupted him with the remark, "Never mind so much talk; just tell the jury what you saw and what was done, and what was the cause of the difficulty between the accused." "You mean what brought about de difficil 'twixt Mose and datudder gemmen, said the witness, pointing to one of the prisoners in the dock. "flint's what I wish to know," remarked the attorney. "Well, boss, if you bleeve me, I never did find out what was de instigation of de circumstance," said the witness. A HINT TO BUDDING SPHAKERS.—It is related of One Job Walmsley, a Yorkshiro advocate of teetotalism, who was humorous in a rough way as well as eloquent, that he was waited upon on one occasion by a young man who was ambitious to shine upon platforms, after the manner of Jabez Inwards, Simeon Smithard, and J. B. Gough. " Tha wants to be a public speyker, dos' tha, lad? And tha thinks awm the chep to put tha up to a wrinkle about it? Tha's reight, I awm ! Now harks ' tha! When tha rises to to mek thy speych, hit taable an' oppen thy mawth. If nowt comes, tak' a sup of watther an' hit taable again. Then oppen thy mawth wider than afoor. Then if nowt comes, tak' thysen off, and leave public speykin' to such as me."—Good Tem- plars' Watchword. It has been said that "genius is an infinite capacity 'for taking pains." This may truly be said of thorough- ness, for no one was ever yet thorough without "taking pains." In purpose they may be; but to carry out their purpose they must take some trouble. There is no royal road to the certainty and assurance which are the results of a real mastery of one's subject, and which are un- shakable by either the assault of sudden questions or unexpected demands for the display of one's power. This can be arrived at only step by step; and those who are looked up to as teachers and advisers, whether as re gards art, science, philanthropic schemes, or any other thing creditable to the individual and useful to the world in general, must inevitably have so advanced—some with longer strides than others, it is true, but all alike making sure of one step before taking another. Among the arts of the West which are making for themselves a new home in Japan is the art of advertising. A bookseller in Tokio, desiring to sell his wares, thus advertised them lately in the newspapers :—" The advan- tages of our establishment-1. Prices cheap as a lottery. 2. Books elegant as a singing-girl. 3. Print clear as crystal. 4. Paper tough as elephant's hide. 5. Cus- tomers treated as politely as by the rival steamship companies. 6. Articles as plentiful as in a library. 7. Goods despatched as expeditiously as a cannon ball. 8. Parcels done up with as much care as that bestowed on her husband by a loving wife. 9. All defects, such as dissipation and idleness, will be cured by young people paying us frequent visits, and they will become solid men. 10. The other advantages we offer are too many for language to express." BOILED EGGS.—The lightest preparation of eggs is to , simply boil them three minutes, when the white will be slightly coagulated, and the yolk will retain its fluid state. A new-laid egg will require longer boiling than a stale one. Four minutes is not too long to get the white well set of a quite fresh egg, while three minutes will be [ generally sufficient for one more advanced. Machines ' may be bought for this purpose, and an egg boiled at the breakfast table by one of these simple tin machines will not fail to give satisfaction. An egg may be boiled 1 hard in from five to ten minutes, but to boil them mealy (which is the lightest preparation next to only boiling them long enough to set the white) allow one whole hour. The experiment should be tested by those who are not aware of the result. It transforms the hard-boiled egg into a digestible article of food.—From 1 Cassell's Cookery. ...

div.head: OUR LON 13( )N LETTER.
div.p: OUR LON 13( )N LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

New members sitting in the House of Commons ! just now have the greatest difficulty in believing that this is the assembly of which they have heard so much. Where are the rows with the Irish mem- bers, the defiance of the Speaker, the cross voting in the lobby, the outrages upon Mr. Gladstone, and the occasional suspension of a member? Nothing of the kind is now known or seen. The House meets at its usual time, gets through the questions, the number of which is the only relic of former times, and then proceeds with the orders of the day which are being disposed of with extraordinary rapidity. There is in fact a truce between conten- ding parties, and nothing is likely to be done till the time comes when Mr. Gladstone makes his statement with respect to Irish affairs. This condi- tion of affairs is not exciting, but it is ex- ceedingly gratifying from a business point of view. If the House only had some business in hand, it would get forward with it with rapidity. There are, however, only the estimates, and the op- portunity is being judiciously used to get them for- ward as quickly as possible. Naturally in the new order of things, Mr. Rylands and one or two others of the old economists turn up again, and take their former place in Committee of Supply. To find Mr. Rylands on his feet is one of the best signs of Parliamentary welfare. During the last Parliament he was for the most part compelled to remain in seclusion. The Irish members had "nobbled" the Committee, and any English member who took part in the purpose- less conversation was regarded as an obstructionist. Mr. Gladstone is in excellent health and spirits, though his voice is no better than it should be. He takes great care of it, rarely uplifting it beyond conversational tone, and sometimes not being quite audible. A peculiarity of his weakness is that the more he uses his voice the better it gets. He always speaks with more vigour towards the end of a speech than he started with. Ile is in the highest spirits, and is more than ever confident of being able to accomplish.his last great work. If the story of his early, struggles, dating from Christmas last, should ever come to be told it would be a record of one of the greatest triumphs achieved by man. • It is not so far back that we can forget the powerful opposition instantly arrayed against Mr. Gladstone when it was known that he was con!Jemplating the introduction of a scheme which would practi- cally give Home Rule to Ireland. It was not the Conservatives he feared. His enemies were those of his own household. When Parliament was on the eve of meeting, and members were gathering at the Reform Club in anticipation of businea com- mencing, I noted in this correspondence the feel- ing of depression that was everywhere prevalent. The most devoted followers of Mr. Gladstone, some of the most fearless Radicals, stood dismayed at this fresh trumpet call. "Even Mr. Gladstone could not do this," they said, " without breaking up the Liberal party. They are beginning now to think that he can. Dunne.' the last two months public opinion, first shocked, has become accustomed to the notion of Ireland, still bound in friendly chains to the empire, caring for her own local affairs. Had Mr. Gladstone submitted his proposals on the first day Parliament met they would inevitably have been rejected. People look upon them now without affright, and by April will be discussing them with as much calmness as if the scheme were a new water bill. This .is an enormous advantage to Mr. Gladstone, and one that will grow as time moves forward, _ _

The tlOod of public opinion still sets turbulently against Sir Charles Dilke. Though one rose from the dead to prove his innocence, he would not be be- lieved. His opportunity fled when he was not put in the witness box, and there does not seem any likelihood of its returning. It has been shown upon indisputable evidence that Sir Charles Dilke. was not only anxious to go into the box, but had brought down his papers with him, and took it for granted that he would be called. It was at the fatal conference held in the luncheon hour that the counsel, taking a dry legal view of the case and in- sisting upon the fact announced by the judge and conceded by the prosecuting counsdl that there was no case agaimt him, won over Mr. Chamberlain to their view, and then all was lost. Sir Charles will eagerly seize the opportunity of atoning for this error should the Queen's Procter intervene. But that I fear is doubtful. In the meantime Sir Charles has not taken his seat in the House since the trial came off. He declines to leave Lon- don, as it would look as if he were running away, but he will keep very quiet. It is Mr. Broadhurst, not Mr. Jesse Collings, who has declined to wear Ministerial dress upon State occasions. Mr. Collings, I believe, has ordered his clothes, and will have "three acres and a cow" em- blazoned in gold letters upon the collar of his levee dress. But Mr. Broadhurst will go neither to the rare balls at Buckingham Palace nor to the State concerts, unless he be allowed to look in in his ordinary dress, which is another mark of his good sense. _ _ _

Great comfort has been given to the Times by the announcement that Lord Yarborough has gone over to the Conservatives. This is a dreadful thing. •But the Liberal party and Mr. Gladstone must try and bear up against it. It is not altogether unexl pected. Lord Yarborough is a considerable land- owner in the neighbourhood of Grimsby. At the General Election he was so far undecided that he

gave a moderate support to his nephew,Mr. Heneage. When, however, Mr. Heneage, on accepting office, went down to offer himself for re-election, his noble relative turned his back upon him. Never- theless Mr. Ileneage won his election by a consider- ably ineareased majority, which seems to show that Lord 'Yarborough-s territorial influence is not so powerful as he thought. The earl is absolutely un- knoWn in political life. He is still young; hardly out of apron strings. . Public attention has in some measure been with- drawn from the proceedings of Lord Yarborough by the claims of other members of the peerage. T i There is something really shocking in reading n the newspapers a statement to the effect that Earl Cairns, at present visiting Cannes, passed through the streets of the town in the lifeboat of his yacht mounted on wheels and drawn by six white horses. It was to have been a team of elephants, but there being no circus within measurable distance the noble lord had to put with ordinary horses. Per contra he had the lifeboat loaded with 10,000 white camelias, imported from Genoa at enormous ex- pense. Amid these flowers Earl Cairns appropri- ately sat, pelted and being pelted with flowers. His lordship, having quite got over his little passion for Miss Fortescue, is now again engaged to be mar- ried, this time to an American lady. But even "Lord Garmoyle's" orgies are innocent Compared with some other occupations indulged in by our hereditary legislators. At the present mo- ment two of the police courts of London are en- gaged in inveatieating charges of fraud against two noble lords. At Lambeth Police Court Lord Hinton is arraigned with two others upon a charge of ob- taining goods by fraud. At Guildhall Lord Graves is charged with conspiracy to obtain money by false pretenc.es, an indictment which now threatens to lapse into the graver one of forgery. Oddly enough the two persons whom Lord Hinton is specifically charged with robbing are two servants in the establishment of a brother peer. In spite of the state of daily terror in which he lives, the Czar has time to grow fat. He has, indeed, of late become so 'obese that he has resolved to undergo a course of training with the object of re- ducing his weight. Mr. Banting having retired from the business, his Majesty has asked Prince Bismarck to lend him his doctor. Some time ago the German Chancellor suddenly began to grow fat. He placed himself under the treatment of Dr. Schwen- ringer, with such happy results that the Czar will now try the medicine man. The art students of Cambridge got good advice from Mr. Rudolph Lehmanns when he warned them against the dangers of the impressionist school. A painter who has done so much good and sound work would naturally regard their. method as "a combination of idleness and impudence." The Prince of the school is about to cross the Atlantic. I wonder what the verdict of New York wiLl be on the lectures of Mr. Whistler. There is a charming directness about American criticism (when it deals with European reputations) that is most valuable in these days of shams. The critics say what they

mean. I hear the salary of a judge may soon be changing recipients. It is not expected Lord Penzance will sit again. His post was one of the nicest pieces of legal patronage which the Chancellor has in his control. The Deanery of Arches is by no means a sinecure, for it needs special leattling, and what is •called..a judicial mind. Lord Penzance filled it

perfectly; he fills it still, for as yet he has not resigned. In old days he and Sir Jasper Selwyn, and Sir John ..arstake, were the handsomest men at the Bar. They used to be called the Three Male Graces. Lord Penzance made an ideal judge of the Divorce Court. His law was always sound, and lie never blundered. The salary of the*Dean of Arches is the same as that of the judges of the Divorce Court—gs,ooo a year.
Idlers to flit (Editor.

- - MRS. AND MR. WIGGAN IN WIDNES. Sir,—l find by some handbills which are being freely distributed abOtit Widnes and Warrington, that Mr. and Mrs Wiggan, who are Evangelists from London, are holding their singing Evangelistic services in that neighbourhood. and will continue about there for about a month. Having met with the Evangelists at different times, held services with them, and thoroughly enjoyed their meetings, I would I like to have a word or two with your readers, so as to urge them t 3 go and listen to them. Their services are of a very pleasing and of a very important character; they have been very successful in their work (amongst those with whom they live and are united in Christian fellowship) 'n r.iviving the power of vital godliness in the church amongst professors of religion, and also in leading many souls to Christ. Mrs Wiggan has a very pleasing way in placing before her hearers the love of God, and the means by which man's peace, happiness, and salva,ton have been procured, and her appeals go at once to the hearts of those who listen to her. Both of the Evaagelists are very forceful and tel- ling in all their addresses. Another attractive power in their services is the sweet and thrilling singing which as a rule characterises them. They have indeed learnt the happy art of reaching the hearts of the people through their ears, by their sweet, soul- stirring sineing. I could say very many kind things about them and their work, but would rather urge your readers to go, listen, and judge for themselves. You will do me a great favour by inserting this letter, and I believe also will help to smooth the way of those who are in their own way striving to do the Lord's work and trying to help and bless their fellow men.—Yours truly, ALPHA.

SOCIAL EQUALITY. Sir,—l am afraid I cannot compliment "Clifford Dix" for having thrown light on the complex social question. On the contrary I must say his letter is calculated to make "confusion worse confounded." We could not wish for a more flagrant instance of the inchoate ideas which some entertain on the social question than the following sentence from Clifford Dix's letter. "The never-ending dispute as to the exact meaning of the words landlord and capitalist may, I think, now be brought to a close, and in its place be substituted a desire to take hold of the social question in some practical form." Clifford Dix seems to be entirely nn- conscious either that the social question, about which be expatiates with such apparent profundity, is a question of the distribution of wealth, or that land and capital are two of the most important factors that influence the distribution of wealth. "Clifford Dix" is evidently one of those marvel- lcmely "practical " personages who would say to the playsi- oiegist and anatomist " Why dispute about the exact struc- ture of the human body, or the exact functions of the verious covens. Keep to the practical question of how to prevent or cure bodily ailments." Or he might say to the meterologists "Cease your never-ending attempts to define the laws which control the winds and storm!, and let us have mcre about the practical art of navigation." Of course, if he were to do this, instead of getting credit for having a " practical " mind, be would be pitied for having a mind so simple that he could not comprehend that the knowledge sought for was essentially necessary to the accomplishment of the desired end—that, in short, a knowledge of physiology and anatomy is essential to the art of preventing and curing disease, and that a knowledge of the controlling causes of the winds and storms is of vital importance to those who practice the art of navigation. So it is with a knowledge of the exact nature, and operations of land and capital. Those who attempted to deal with the social problem— which is the problem of the distribution of wealth—without this knowledge would be as liable to blunder as a man who attempted to cure diseases without the exact knowledge phymicians are expected to have. So far then from the meaning of the words landlord and capitalist being of no importence, it is really all important. In turning to Mr. Chapman's letters, I must confess at the outaet that I hardly understand what his contentions are. It is useless te bandy phrases to which we each attach differ- ent meanings, and therefore in order to clear matters up I am ebligel cc fall back on the privilege be has availed him- self of so freely, that is of asking questions. In the first place I ask then, does Mr. Chapman still maintain that there is no differeuce between capital and land, that in fact they are the same in their nature and operations? I maintain that they are totally different in their nature, and that the amount of the returns up n each is regulated by entirely different principles. If I own a piece of land and also a certain amount of Capital, the annual return or rent of the former is determined by the margin of cultivation; but the annual return or interest of the latter is fixed by oven competition. I hold the piece of land to the exclusion of everybody else, but thousands of others hold capital in every respect as g.,)od as mine. The rent of the land may be doubled every year through the growth of population or increase of indus- try in its neighbourhood, and not from any effort of my own ; but the interest on my capital is kept down by the competition of others. As a landlord I would exact a con- stantly increasing share of the produce of their labour from others, simply because I had a monopoly of a piece of land, but as a capitalist I would get no larger interest than was considered an equitable return in an open market. Does Mr. Chapman admit or deny these distinctions between land and cepital ? Me next question is,does Mr: Chapman admit or dispute the teachings of the evolutionists? These assert that all living things, men included, tend to increase in numbers be- yond the means of subsistence. If this be so it is utterly fatal to Communistic theories. The Communist proposes to provide for the wants of all, but according to the evolu- tionist that is impossible, as human beings would multiply beyond the means of subsistence ; and therefore if in a com- munal state all were equally provided for, it would mean that all would have the equal privilege of starving. Mr. Chapman says mankind hears a close resemblance to plants. An unfortuttate comparison this for Mr. Chapman, because, if I remember aright, it was his experiments with plants and grasses that helped Darwin very materially to verify his theory of the "struggle for existence." JAQUES.

div.head: RAILWAY TARIFFS AND MADE.
div.p: RAILWAY TARIFFS AND MADE.

Sir,—" Trade Depression" threatens to become a some- what hackneyed saying, and, were it not, that with it, we have an active and positive evil, making itself felt in the shape of streets crowded with unemployed, it is is just pos- sible we should "grin and abide." This course is however impossible ; fathers ef families will not stand by and see their children starve, neither will capitalists watch their capital waste away without doing something to avert the evil. It is well to arrange for relief committees, and to dole out soup. There may be wisdom in granting the unemployed 6s per week for doing nothing in preference to 7s 6d for breaking stones, yet to the present writer, the whole pro- ceeding seems to lack in utility. The supremacy of England in the questions of produc- tion and distribution is being questioned; other nations are 'craning every nerve to oust us from foreign markets, and if they are successful, what is now considered an abnormal state of depression may become normal, and relief commit- tees and soup kitchens will not be able to cope with the evil. It is not enough to find fault with what are mere patiations, and I hope no apology is needed in pressing upon your readers the great necessity that exists for workingmen ardently directing their attention to the several Questions that are injuriously affecting trade. There are men so peculiarly constituted as to imagine that a man calling himself a landlord and owning the land surface, has also a right to own such of nature's products as may be beneath the surface. Such men are to be pitied, but they must not be allowed to hinder in the work of wresting from the landlords the right to charge royalties so exorbitant that British trade is endangered. As a means of transport to and fro in the land, and fur- ther helping in distributing the manufactured article to the world, the railways seem to be the Alpha and omega of trade. Without them we could have no business relations with the outer world. From this it may easily be seen how necessary it is that the nation and not the individual shall own the great iron ways of the land. Throughout the mid- land towns taking Birmingham as a centre, a persistent and what I think wiil now be a successful, campaign, has been carried on, the object being a reduction of tariffs. But this is not sufficient ; no reduction of tariffs the rail- ways are likely to make will enable manufacturers to hold their own, or keep them from making fresh demands upon their workmen. The railways must be worked and owned by the State : working exoenses only must be sought for.

Throughout Germany, the railways are fast becoming the property of the State; in most cases from the outset they have been built and owned by the state. In Prussia within the last ten years nearly the whole of the private lines have been purcoasediby the Government,);and private lines in Prussia and Saxony are administered by the respec- tive governments. Mutual arrangements between the Governments and the respective companies have ended in the former becoming owners, and strange to say, an increase of revenue. This may he acconated for from the fact that all the lines being of one guage, the rolling stock is avail- able at all points, and the transit of "empties " is therefore reduced to a minimum.

The whole of the Continental railway system is reduced to the simplest proportions, a pamphlet of 76 pages being found sufficient do contain the whole of the general tariff, and regulations of the goods traffic. I should fancy in Eng- land that an ordinary Bradshaw will be simplicity itself compared to the rip.e3 and regulations of the London and Neith-Western Railway Company.
In England foreign produce is invited by special and more favourable tariffs ; not so in Girmany, foreign or na- tive, all pay the same rates.

_ I find the great objection to State ownership of the rail- ways is, that it will lead to jobbery, and, as a consequence, to a worse system of administration, resulting in an in- creased cost of carrying. This has not been the case in Germany. Since the States have become owners of the railways great reductions in tariffs have resulted. Local ad- ministrative and consultative bodies manage the State rail- ways, and District Railway Boards settle all disputes, which rarely occur. Nominally the railways are under Imperial control, but practfc4lly they are subject to the laws and regulations of the different States through which they pass.

The various departments nominate members who consult and advise with the minister, and thirty members elected by the various provinces and cities of the kingdom; all holding office for three years. From this it will be seen that a flm grip is kept on the management, and traders find ,t to their interest ta make profits out of manufacturing and not out of distributing goods.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY, 27, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY, 27, 1886.
FUNERAL OF MRS. GARNETI', AT PENKETII.

On Wednesday morning the village of Penketh presented a rather sombre appearance, the blinds being drawn down at most of the residences; the respect seemed to prevail in rich and poor alike to the memory of Mrs. Garnett, of Vine House, Pen- keth, relict of the late Robert Garnett, whose death preceded that of his widow by nearly nine years. Mrs. Garnett died on Saturday afternoon last, aged 85 years and 10 months. She had been confined to her bedroom for some months, and quietly passed i away n the midst of her assembled children. Her husband, Mr. Robt. Gardett, sen., was the founder of the firm of cabinet makers, R. Garnett and Sons, of Penketh and Warrington. The deceased Mrs. Gar- nett was a rare help-meet to her hushand, and when the business was in its infancy she took an active share in its promotion. She was a skilful needle- woman and a shrewd saleswoman, while the making up of the upholstery, curtains, carpets, &c., came under her supervision. The funeral cortege started from her late residence in the following order :—The male employes of Messrs. R. Garnett and Sons, num- bering over 40, headed by the two foremen, Mr. Thomas Garnett, jun., of Penketh, and Mr. William Nicholson, of Warrington. next followed the re- mains of the deceased in a beautiful brass-mounted coffin, the wood being polished and elaborately finished, .and made by deceased's second son, Mr. William Garnett (Garnett and Company), Bridge-street Row, Chester. The coffin was covered on the top and sides with floral wreaths, tastefully made by the daughters and granddaughters of the deceased, on each wreath being a last loving tribute written by the handy- workers. The remains were carried by relays of workmen, some of whom had been employed by the firm 30 or 40 years, and one so. long as half a century. In the rear of the coffin the male relatives followed on foot, Mr. Robert Garnett, J.P., Mr. David Garnett, and Mr. William Garnett, of Ches- ter (three Sons); after whom came the sons-in- law, Mr. James Fildes, of Stretford, Mr. Robert Jenks, of London; Mr. Joseph Thonley, brother of deceased; next, grandsons, Mr. Robert Edward Garnett, Mr. Sydney Garnett, Mr. Robert Fildes and Mr. Samuel Flicks, Mr. John William Garnett, Master Fred. Payne Garnett, Master Phillip Gar- nett; also Mr. Dowd, Mr. Smith, of llelsby, other relatives and friends, amongst whom were Mr. Lan- caster, Mr. Thomas Briscoe, Mr. John Thornley, of Hyde, Mr. B. Hobson, Mr. Summersgill, Mr. John Mainley, Mr. James Watson, Rev. James McTurk, Rev. G. E. Cutting, Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Seed, Mr. Thomas Garnett, senr., Mrs. John Johnson, Mr. Robert Davies and Mr.. Thomas S. Smith, M. 8., Warrington, Mr. John 11. Gornall, J.P., and Mrs. Gornall, of Penketh Lodge, and a large concourse of neighbours and friends. Next followed the, female relatives in mourning coaches. In the first coach were the daughters, Mrs. T. Coop, of South- port, Mrs. Fildes, Stretford, Mrs. Jenks, London and Mrs. Robert Gannett; second coach, Mrs. David Garnett, Mrs. William Garnett, Mrs. Dowd, Miss Garnett; third coach, Miss Mary Garnett, Miss Nellie Garnett, Miss F. Garnett, Miss Moses; in fourth coach were Miss A. Moses, Miss Briscoe, and fifth coach, Mrs. Briscoe, Miss Alice Gandy, Miss Jane Gandy; sixth coach, Mr. R. Garnett; private carriage with members and relatives of the family therein; also followed Mr. Edward Parker's con- veyance, and the closed -carriages of Mrs, Ockle- shaw, Greystone House, and Mrs. Mary Tinsley, Three Elms. Arriving at the Penketh Wesleyan Chapel, a short service was gone through by the Rev. James McTurk, and the Rev. G. E. Cutting, after a hymn had been sung, offered prayer; Mr. McTurk following with an impressive and solemn address. There was a large congregation present, the pews being filled. On the conclusion of the service the remains were brought out of the chapel and the procession reformed, being augmented on the way, and on arriving at Sankey Chapel, Great Sankey, the numbers were further increased by a large concdrurse of friends who waited in the. grave yard. The Rev. Edwin Sandys Jackson, vicar of Great Sankey, met the cortege at the church gates, and, proceeding into the church, conducted the funeral service with psalm and lesson suitable for the occasion, afterwards going .through the usual service at the grave yard. On conclusion, the people joined in singing the well-known hymn— " Rock of ages cleft for me." The children of the Wesleyan Day School were formed in a line on each side of the road passing the school, and the chil- dren at the Penketh Infant School also stood In line as the procession passed by. The respect in which the deceased was held greatly heightened the impressiveness of the funeral.

C. D. i and Princess of Battenburg, arrived in London from Wind- ' sor on Friday afternoon, and attended the performance of IGonnod's new oratorio, " More et Vita," at the Albert Hall. There wet, a large and distinguished audience. Her Majesty seemed in best of health and spirits. • CRUEL HOAX ON THE UNE3IPLOYED.—A cruel hoax has been perpetrated on a large number of men out of work liv- ing in distant towns. Ward was sent around that the Man- chester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company were about to commence the erection of a bridge across the Dee at Connah's Quay, for which they possess powers, and men in numbers (tom Liverpool, Manchester, and the Midlands have been arriving, only, after many weary miles' tramp, to learn they have been fooled. THE PIMLICO MYSTERY.—The adjourned magisterial ex- amination into the Pimlico mystery was resumed on Friday at Westminster Police Court, when Mrs. Adelaide Bartlett (30) was again charged with causing the death of her hus- band, aed the Rev. George Dyson (27), Wesleyan minister, Wes charged with being an accessory before the fact. Fur- ther evidence was given as to the movements of the de- ceased and his wife at Claverton-street, Pimlico, where the murder was alleged to have been committed. Mrs. Doggett, landlady of the house, spoke to frequent visits of Dyson ; and the deceased told her the night before he was found dead he thought the worst was over, and that he was getting better. On the same night Mrs. Bartlett, inquiring if witness had taken chloroform, said her husband was in the habit of taking ten drops to make him sleep, but she should not hesitate to give him twelve. That was said in the presence of the deceased. A servant in the employ of Mrs. Doggett also gave evidence as to the visits of Mr. Dyson. She had seen him and Mrs. Bartlett sitting to- gether on the floor and on the couch. Once Mrs. Bartlett was sitting on the floor with her head resting on the knee of Mr. Dyson, who was sitting in a low chair. .Other evi- dence was given, and the case was adjourned until next day.
THE--CASE OF MR. lONGSHAW.

On Thursday, at Warrington County Court, Mr.. A. Browne made application to his Honour Judge Ffoulkes in regard to the case of Mr. Longshaw, who is undergoing imprisonment for con- tempt of court. Mr. Brown said he had that morn- ing received the accounts from Ilie bankrupt witch were required to be filed. As there was not another sitting of the Court for three weeks, he asked his Honour to make some airangement in order to facilitate the release of the bankrupt before that time.—His Honour said Mr. Browne did not seem to realise what contempt of Court meant. It was a serious offence, and defendant had been guilty of flagrant contempt, as he had no excuse to urge for his conduct. If the accounts were satisfactory to the Court and the official receiver the bankrupt would be released from prison.—Mr. Browne: I am not ap- plying for his discharge; but seeing that the time is so long before the next court is held, and before I can make another application, I ask your Honour if some arrangement might not be made to take the application sooner ?—The Registrar observed that the next court would be held on the 18th of March. —His Honour said if the accounts were satisfactory he should not detain the bankrupt any longer than necessary. He could not make any order then, or give any directions. The accounts had been fur- nished, and be should recommend Mr. Browne to see the Official Receiver.—Mr. Browne said the bankrupt could not be released from prison until his Honour received an application.—His Honour: No discharge can be granted until he has purged his con- tempt by doing that which was required of him.— Mr. Browne: There is no court until the 18th of March, and I cannot make any application for his release until then.—His Honour: I cannot help that; it has been brought upon him by his own conduct. —Mr. Browne said that Mr. Longshaw had already been in prison fire weeks.—His Honour remarked that it did not matter whether the bankrupt had been in a longer time, for he could not alter his de- cision. The sooner the accounts were furnished the sooner he would be released.—Mr. Browne: I have them in my hands.—His Honour :1 cannot help that. They must have the Official Receiver's sanction.— The application was not granted. MARKETS.
"BREAD OR BULLETS."

PARIS, FRIDAY —The Socialist organs to-day publish a telegram from Calais stating that 2,000 unemployed men met at St. Pierre. and demanded help. Placards have been posted bearing the words, "Bread or bullets." At the close of the meeting the police dispersed the mob, but another meeting has been fixed for Sunday. HEAVY SNOWFALL IN PARIS.

PARIS, FRIDAY.—Snow began to fall heavily this morn- ing, and has now reached a considerabbi depth. In spite of the admi-able organisation for clearing the streets here there has been some interruption of traffic. The cold is intense, as it is freezing hard. TURCO-BULGARIAN CONVENTION.

BUCHAREST, FRIDAY.-It is stated on good authority that the text of the single article of which the Turco. Bulgarian Convention, proposed by Madjid Pacha and M. Gueshoff, consists is as follows :—Peace between Servia and Bulgaria is restored. The present treaty to be ratified 15 days after signature. The Servian reply to this proposa is expected to-day.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.

The House met at 4 O'clock. Lord GraaNvutz, replying to Lord Sidmouth, said he bad no objection to give a return of the Naval military officers employed in the colonies by permission of the War Office and Admiralty. He would also give a return of the ships, guns, and military stores given to the colonies and making troops interchangeable.—The Duke of Cemßulpou hoped as many compulsorily retired officers as possible would find emp'oyment in colonies. The House adjourned at ten minutes past five. HOUSE OF COMMONS The House met at four o'clock.

QUESTIONS.—Mr. HOWARD VINCENT gave notice that on the army and navy estimates he should call attention to the requirements of the volunteer force, and move a resolu- tion for the increase of the capitation grant.—Mr. J. Mon- LEY, replying to Mr. B. Kelly, eAid the report of Mr. Steven- son on Doregal harbour works was under consideration.— Mr. CHILDERS, replying to Sir R. Fowler, said when the letter accepting Sir E. Henderson's resignation of the office of Chief Commissioner of Police was despatched, a note ac- companied it acknowledging the long services of Sir Ed- mund ; and he had every reason to believe he was satisfied with that recognition of his services. His pen- sion had not yet been awarded Sir Edmund Henderson. The ATTORNEY-GENERAL, replying to Mr. Baumann, said he attended the banquet at the Criterion to the labour representatives. He positively denied that there was general hissing when Her Majesty's health was proposed. The statements published were gross • xaggera- tions.—Lord HOBHOUSE and the member for Burnley (Mr. Rylands) who were present, also 'denied that there was his- sing on the occasion. THE LONDON RIOTS.—On the motion to go into Com- mittee of Supply, Mr. J. STUART called attention to the late riots in the metropolis, and moved that in the opinion of the House no reform of ,the administration and organisa- tion of the metropolitan police force would be satisfactory unless provision was made for such reforms of the govern- ment of the metropolis as would ensure to the representa- tives of tbe ratepayers of the metropolis a direct control over their own police. He expressed the opinion that much as local self-government was required, thosit who held the command of the police would always be masters of the sit- nation.—Lord A. PERCY opposed the resolution, and de- fended the police.—Mr. HOWELL referred to the fact that, in 1884, a procession of 130,000 persons marched from Blackfriars Bridge to Hyde Park, and not one window was broken or plant destroyed, the reason being that those who got up the demonstration had tne confidence of the working classes. If control of police were hauded over to municipal government the safety of the Metropolis would be perfect.—Mr. Bunmen-Corrrrs severely con- demned the manner in which the resignation of Sir E. Hen- derson had been brought about.—Mr. CHILDERS explained in detail the communications that had passed between himself and the police authorities immediatety after he entered on the duties of the Home Office. Regarding the resignation of Sir E. Henderson, he said no one could more regret the resignation and the causes that had led to it.— Mr. W. H. Smith was of opinion that, notwithstanding all ' that had been said, blame rested with the authorities.—Mr. BRADLAUGH said if the public inquiry was granted he undertook to show that for six weeks prior to the meeting large sums were paid by leading Conservative members of Hoth Houses of Parliament by cheque and money to Samuel Peters, one of the organizers of the demonstration.—Mr. HOWARD VINCENT bore testimony to the mode in which Sir E. Henderson had for 17 years performed his duties.

At a large meeting of Scotch ironmasters in Glasgow on Wednesday it was unanimously agreed that steps should be taken to restrict the production of pig iron. TZRRIBLE ACCIDENT.—On the London, Chatham, and Dover Railway on Saturday, near Reculver, the driver of a down train, after travelling some distanco below Herne Bay, discovered that something was wrong, and found the dead body of Mr. George Carey, hanging in front of the locomo- tive. Mr. Carey is a well-known agriculturist in East Kent, and was about forty years of age. Deceased had a fearful gash across the forehead, and both legs were broken. He had evidently been carried over a mile from the spot , where the occurrence happened, which is close to the farm / be occupied.

div.head: DROWNING OF A WARRINGTON
div.p: THE DROWNING OF A WARRINGTON
GENTLE MAN.

In our last issue we recorded the death by drown- ing, at Oxford, of Mr. Edward Schonberg, son of the Rev. M. Schonberg, vicar of St. Peter's, Warrington, and an exhibitioner of Exeter College. For several years the deceased gentleman attended the Warring- ton Grammar School. At the inquest, respecting the sad occurrence, which was held yesterday week in the hall of Exeter College, Mr. J. E. Quibell, undergradu • ate of Carist Church, Mr. H. E. D. Hammond, under- graduate of Corpus Christi, and Mr. Earnest A. Glover gave evidence, from which it appeared that on Thursday afternoon the latter gentleman and the de- ceased went on the upper river in a boat. Deceased rowed, and Mr. Glover steered. After they had changed once or twice, they were trying to do so again, when deceased slipped, caught his foot in a hole in the floor, of the boat, and it overturned. A man who was on the bank put his scull into the water for him to seize, but he was not able to do so. Glover was reseued by Mr. Hammond. Deceased was got out of the river half an hour after, but all efforts to • restore animation failed. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and reque=ted the coroner to forward to the Tice-Chancellor recommendations that a sufficient staff of water police be plac.,d on the upper river and lifebelts and ropes placed at frequent inter- vals on the bank.

The funeral of Mr. Ed ward Schonberg took place on Monday in St. Sepulchre's Cemetery, Oxford. The first portion of the burial service was read in the col- lege chapel, where an appropriate hymn was also sung, and a funeral aaarch played on the organ. A procession was then formed, comprising the Rev. T. A. Schonberg, of Blackburn and Oriel College, and Mr. Alfred Schonberg, of Warrington, brothers of the deceased, as chief mourners ; the fellows, sewlars; exhibitioners, and commoners of the college ; some members of other colleges who were educated at Man- chester Grammar School, where the deceased received his early education, besides several officials and ser- vants of Exeter. Handsome wreaths from sorrowing friends were placed on the coffin. Preaching at St. Paul's Church on Sunday evening, the vicar (the Rev. S. Wilkinson) made a touching reference to the accident. The deceased gentleman, he said, was a young man whom they all knew, all loved, and all respected. The last time he (the preacher) saw him was after he had been assisting in one of their parochial entertainments in connection with their mothers' meeting, and as he shook hands with and thanked him for his help, he little thought that that would he the last time he should see him in this world. Of him it could not be said that he was idle. He had led a busy, active life. He worked hard in the Warrington Grammar School, at the Man- chester Grammar School, a+ the Vie.oria University, and within the lart few months proceeded to the Uni- versity at Oxford, which it had been his ambition for many years to enter. When life was opening before him, when all was looking so beautiful, and when his prospects were becoming so ripe, Almighty God in his goodness had taken him away—taken him, they believed, from the evil to come. He asked their prayers and sympathy for the bereaved family, and urged them to work while they had time, because the night cometh when no man can work." At the con- clusion of the service the organist played tbe " Dead March" in "Saul,' the congregation meanwhile rem alnico. seated. The Pall Mall Gazetk, commenting on the accident, says :—ln London a man drowning in the presence of an unconcerned crowd is a common sight enough. But one would hardly expect to find the policy of " laisser faire, laisser noyer," prevailing in Oxford also. Such, however, would seem to be the case from the evidence given at the inquest upon the Exeter undergraduate who was drowned a day or two ago in the Upper River. "There were several people on the bank, but no attempt was-made to rescue him." That being so, the coroner's jury were certainly right in recom- mending the Vice-Chancellor to have a sufficient staff of water-police placed on the Upper River with life. belts and ropes at frequent intervals. Short of the entrance examination in swimming to which all boat- ing men at Cambridge have to submit, this is the very least the Oxford authorities can do. The -Illy won- der is that it has not been done long ago. The Ucpor River is supposed, rightly or wronoy, to be the pre- serve of the muffs, who, one would have imagined, required protection against accidents more and not less than their athletic brethren on the Lower River.

WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB. A meeting of the commitiee of the above club was held on Wednesday afternoon in the clibroom, White Bull, Warrington. The chairman, Mr. Marsh pre- sided, and there was a large attendance.

TEE WAGES QUESTION. -- Toe first business on the agenda paper was to consider the wages question—its relation to the present prices of agricultural produce and the cost et living.—The SECRE- TARY (Mr. J. L. Stelfox) stated that in France the average amount of cellos received by a farm labourer in 1872—and it is not greatly differeet now—was £6 16s 9d a year In addition to hoard, nd if to this was added the value of the food consumeo by the labourer, calculated at 41d a day, it appeared that the maintenance of a farm labourer in France costs his employer, on an average, about £l4 3s 2d per • annum. Mr. Stelfox then stated that the chairman reques- ted him to open the discussion on the wages question. The wages question, he considered, should be treated on very much the same lines as the rent question. If certain wages were paid 10 years ago could it be reasonably expected that those wages should be paid now ? What was the difference in the farmers' position now from what it was 10 years ago, and out of what fund did the farmer obtain the money with which he paid the wages? Of course these wages were paid from the money the far- mer received for the sale of his produce, and it is known that 10 years ago the produce of a farm would realise 30 per cent more money than it did now. (Hear, hear, and "Quite that.") Therefore if the farm labourer was to re- ceive his living out of produce of the soil, the farmers' source of income being so much contracted the labourer could enlv expect that a similar contraction should be applied to his source of living. But that was only, one view to take of the Labour question, because whatever the labourer was receiv- ing 10 years ago, as they had said over and over again at that club, the wages he now received had_a far larger purchasing Value than it had then. Suppose 153 was the wage paid 10 years ago to the labourer, that 15s now is of a purchasing value equal to 18s or 19s. There, then, were two solid reasons on which the farmer could base his claims to a reasonable reduction in the wages of farm labourers. There ' was another point which could reasonably be brought to the notice of farm labourers in connection with that wages question, and that was that the farmer must obtain his pro- duce at such a cost that he could bring it into the market to compete with foreign produce, and when they found that l in other countries, such as France, the farmer can obtain his farm labourers eit a total cost of only £l4 3s 2d per annum, . that was 58 8d a week, it showed that if farming was to con- ; tinue in this country the farm labourer must be willing to assimilate his position to some extent to the position of farm labourers in foreign countries. Now the practical question for that club was to consider what they could recommend farmers to reduce the wages of their labourers by. *There are two classes of farm labourers, the English ! and the Lish, and considering the cost of living, and also the price that was obtained for agricultural produce, he thought a general reduction of from 2s to 3s per week in both English and Irish farm , labourers' wages would be fair and reasonable. (Hear, hear.) He did not think there was any member of the club who desired to make the farm labourers' position , worse than it is now, but if ths labourer was to improve his , position he must seek for that improvement elsewhere than in higher wages. He could only obtain his fair share from the profit obtained from the produce of the soil. If the farm labourer who wanted to improve his position obtained some small allotment he would then be in the position of some of the labouring men in towns who held small shops which were looked after by their wives and families. If a farm labourer was in such a position that his wife and family could attend to any small allotment that might be the means of recovering for him tome of that benefit which had been taken'away frem him by the reduction of wages that the failing prices of farm produce will necessitate. (Elear,tear.)—A MEMBER thought it would be better to allow the wages of farm labourers to come to a proper level of themselves as they had always hitherto done. If a farmer paid his labourers the same wages he has done for some years back that was his own look-out. He believed it was for each individual farmer to begin to reduce wages himself, but if they as .a club put themselves into the posi- tion of trying to drop wages he thought they would raise up a good deal of feeling against them. (Hear, Isear.)—A MEMBER did not agree with the Secretary's remarks about allotments. When they paid a labourer a full day's wages they wanted in return a full day's work—(mer, hear)—but from his own experience be found that labour- ers who had land of their own got up in the morning and worked at it. and afterwards came tired to the work for which they were paid. They came to that work to rest themselves, and towards night they again rested before going hack to their own allotments. Therefore he (the member) aid not go in so strongly for the small allotment business as a good many people did (Hear, hear.) The sec retary bad suggested a redection of wages of 2s or 33 a week, but that reduction was hardly equal to the reduction in the price of agricultural produce.— file Seca-err/lov ex- plained that he did not mean that the allotments should occupy the time of the labourer birneelf, but of his family. If a labourer did not work properly it was the farmer's OWE fault.—A MEMBER said be had always been in favour of labourers having garden allotments, but now he found they would not take the trouble to dig them, and labourers said It was cheaper to buy potatoes than grow them.— The discussion was continued at some length, and one mem- ber remarked that if the wages were lowered too much it would be a premium to dishonesty; they must make the landlords meet them better, in order that they might pay fair wages to their men. He also expressed the conviction that to work farms without beer allowance was a very satis- factory method, a view in which he was secon- ded by another farmer, whilst others held that a litttle allowance of beer at certain times was necessary. Ultimately it was decided to recommend to the general meeting of the club that farmers in this district should re- quire characters from their labourers, English and Irish ; that a week's notice be given and taken ; and that farmers should concert measures for obtaining a fair reduction in the rate of wages. The question whether farmers in the district should be recommended to engage labourers upon, a fixed rate of wages, without giving anything in kind, was also discussed, and it was thought that that course should as far as practicable be followed out. The meeting then adjourned.
The new Vice-Chamberlain, Lord Kilconrsie, was on Wednesday, re-elected witbont opsosition for South Somer- set.
Several thousand wild ducks were seen on the north shore of the Clyde, near to Cardross, an Sunday, indicating severe winter weather outside.

Two colliers were killed in coalpits near Ruabon, on Wed- nesday, and in both cases by the same agency—the sudden collapse of overhead mineral. The Divorce Court, on Thursday, on the application of the wife, Elizabeth Malcolm, annulled the marriage of Jas. Malcolm, who was convicted of bigamy by marrying Miss Dash, at Brighton. While engaged pulling down an old brick wall at Bury on Wednesday, a labourer named Patrick Burns was killed, and a fellow-workman named Patrick Shannon, it is feared, fatally injured. A Tows NEARLY BURNED DOWN.—A serious fire began at Wilmington, South Carolina, on Sunday afternoon, on the river steamer Bladen, which set fire to wharves and sheds. A high wind was blowing, which carried the flames through buildings saturated with turpentine. Two steamers, three blocks of stores, many private residences, two railway goods stations, two mills, a church, and other buildings were completely destroyed. The loss i 8 estimated at a mil- lion and a half dollars.

WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.—A sitting of this Court was held before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes on Thursday morning. The business was light. Mr. H. J. Longton, solicitor, applied for a new trial in the case of David Irving v. Edward and Selina Armitage, which was a claim for money lent, heard at the last Court ; it was rather a complicated matter, and he brought the case before the Court as much for direction as anything else. The grounds of the defence were that the money was spent for drink and not food, which was a complete surprise to his client, as he had lent the money to pay debts with, and had a witness to swear that it was lent for the purchase of food. He asked that the plaint be amended as against Edward Armitage, but his Honour said that he could not amend the plaint as judgment had been (-riven. Mr. Longton then asked that a new trial should be ordered for part of the claim, but his Honour declined to ac- cede to the application.—Thomas Davies, Howard- street, Sankey Bridges, was committed to prison for 40 days for not paying arrears under an adrain- tration order, his Honour 'directing that if the debtor paid 30a the warrant would not be issued. A similar order was made on Thomas F. Wood, of 77, Wel lfield-street.! THE SHOCEING DEATH OF A COLLTEH—Mr. Brig- house, coroner, resumed an inquiry at the Feathers Inn,St. Helen', on Monday afternoon, into the circumstances atten- ding the death of Edward Spence, twenty-seven ye an of a„,,, which took place in No. 11 pit, Ravenhead Collieries, on the sth inst., under circumstances previously reported. Hedley, inspector of mines, Mr. Glover, miners' agent, and Mr. F. France. colliery manager, were present. It appeared that deceased worked as drawer to George Marsh. who in his evidence expressed the opinion that there had been a slop of earth from the side, which had pushed out one or two props. The timber was quite new, and none was broken by the accident.—James Guest, foreman. said he examined- the place about twelve o'clock and found it perfectly safe. The working places of the men were not examined immediately prior to the night men going down.—Mr. France said an examination was made about three o'clock in the afternoon; while the daymen were at work. The fireman went round again during the night. He thought that was in accordance with the requirements of the Act, and was what Mr. Hall, her Majesty's Inspector of Mines, ap- proved of.—The coroner did not see how on evidence anyone could say that there was a proper inspection.—Mr. France said the fireman was constantly going through the place.—Mr. Hedley stated that M. Hall (Government In- spector) had made an examination, and wished him to say that, so far as the place was concerned, he had no fault to find.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death," and added a presentment that the evidence showed an insuf- ficient inspection of the said colliery, and suggested an in- spection as soon as possible both before the day and night shift men went to walk. LYMAL SOMER.—On Wednesday evening a soiree was held connection with the Lymm Conservative Association. Tblj was a good number present, and a pleasant evening " spent. Cetoert CONCERT.—On Monday evening the annual ee concert in connection with Lymm Congregational Schc% was held in the school-room, when the chair was occePl'A by the Rev. Mr. Houston. There was a good attandanee'„e programme of glees, songs, pianoforte and banjo solos, readings was gone through, amongst the contributors belisei Mc. T. Sperling, Miss Podmore, Mr. A. Brymer, Mr. Chz'r Stewart, Misses Astley and Ellison, and the choir, &c. THE MASSEY BROOK Worms.—On Monday, a neeetitjg of Lymrn ratepayers was held at the Spread Eagle Inn, business being "to consider the application made by Mes2ke Gibson and Co. in reference to the Massey Brook VW:, and to pass resolntihns thereon." Mr. E. A. Burrows P`iwt, sided, and amongst those present were Messrs. J. George Hall, Frederick Holt, Edward Burrows, E. M. u,r7r, field, H. S. Saville, E. Gibbons, Thomas Griffiths, J. elough, H. Atkinson, J. Ross, J. Hatton, H. Collins, &C."i„g Chairman read a letter from Messrs. Gibson and CO. Stat7,l that they were asking for powers from the Lyme, I.le-e Board to carry on a soap and starch manufactory, would employ a large number of men and boys. Some reo dents of Lymm and Thelwall protested against the sornd on the ground that they would be injurious to health aei vegetation, but they (Messrs. Gibson) stated that no Elh; cue gases would arise, and they were prepared to pay fall market value for any crops that could be shown to been damaged by their works. Mr Holt proposed " Tb3o this meeting, whilst wishful that the Board shall not 1:10 anything that would be injurious to the permanent interes, of the parish, is of opinion that if it can be shown `s,4 stated by Mr. Gibson) that there will he no noxious vapetly, detrimental to either health or vegetation, arising frotn tbea works, the Board be earnestly requested to grant the applied for by Messrs. Gibson and Co., and so consider interests of the many as against the interest, of the feici, Mr. Levi Jackson seconded the resolution, which was e 2„,, red. It was resolved that Mr. Holt's resolution, toot."' with a petition in favour of the works, be laid before °. Board by Mr. Hall.

APPETISING DAINTY DISHES MADE I WITH EGGS. FRENCH PANCAKES. Take half a pound of flour, half an ounce of baking pow- der, one ounce of melted butter, one ounce of soft sugar, two eggs, and pinch of salt, and grated lemon peel, with suffi- cient milk to form a soft batter. Fry and sprinkle sugar on top, roll up, and serve hot. LEMON CRBAM. Peel three lemons and squeeze out the juice into one quart of milk. Add the peel, cut in pieces, and cover the mixture for a few hours, then add six eggs well beaten, and one pint of water well sweetened, strain, and simmer over a gentle ire till it thickens. Serve very cold. LEMON CUSTARDS. The yolks of four eggs, the whites of two, one cup of sugar, one cup of cold water, one spoonful of butter, and one spoonful of corn starch, Wended in a little cold water, and the grated peel and juice of a large lemon. Bake in cups and frost with the whams. BAKED APPLE PUDDING. Peel, core, and slice a dozen or more tart apples ; put them into a saucepan with half a-pound of butter and stew them ; then add four eggs, beaten a little, and the grated rind of one lemon and a little grated nutmeg; sweeten to your taste; now line a pie-dish with paste, pour in your mixture and bake.

MINCED BEEF. Cut the meat from the bones; then break the bones up and put them in a stew-pan with onion, carrot, thyme, and two cloves; moisten with a quart of water, and boil gently until reduced to less than half; and when done strain, , remove all greise and make this into rather less than half a pint of good sauce. Chop the beef fine, put it with the sauce in a stew-pan, add a little grated lemon peel, a very little nutmeg and a teaspoonful of any good sauce. Stir over the fire until quite hot, and serve with poached eggs placed round the mince. LEMON PATTIES. Boil the thin yellow rind of two or three lemons in water till they become quite soft; then pound them to a paste ; melt quarter of a pound of butter, and stir into it a quarter of a pound of powdered sugar; when well mixed, add the lemon paste, beat up the yolks of six eggs, add these and the juice of two lemons to the other ingredients, line a sufficient number of patty pans %vith puff paste, fill these with the above mixture, and bake in a hot oven for twenty-five minutes. ROCK CAKE. Mix two pounds of finely-powdered sugar and the whites of seven eggs; beat them well together, then add and mix with them two pounds of sweet almonds, blanched and cut lengthwise into fillets; form the mixture with the hands into cones about the size of the inside of an ordinary wine glass; place them at a littl‘ distance apart on sheets of white paper, laid upon biking tins and bake, or rather dry them, in a moderate oven; when cold they may be easily removed from the paper.

Add twe spoonfuls ef any good !duo°, a pinch of pepper, a little nutmeg, and the juice of a lemon; toes the whole well together over the fire, and when the eggs are , hot dish them up and serve. flOgla • •,• 4 f,r'' . E OMELET WITH FINE HERBS. Break three eggs in a basin; to these add a spoenfnl of cream, a small pat of butter broken in small pieces, a little chopped parsley and shalot, some popper and salt; then put two ounces of butter into your omelet, and put over the fire. While the butter is melting whip the eggs, tEe., well togeter until they become frothy, as soon as the butter be- gang to fritter, pour the eggs into the pan, and stir the omelet; as the eggs appear to set and become firm, roll the omelet into the form of an oval cushion; allow it to ac- quire a golden colour on one side over the fire, and the" turn it out on its dish; pour a little thin sauce or gravy under it and serve. Two tablespoonfuls of flour, the whites of two eggs, and the yolk of one, with sufficient milk to moisten; beat well together, and boil for twenty minutes. Serve with sugar. -• , F BAKED EGGS. These form a nice breakfast dish. Butter a tin or earthen pie plate and sprinkle it liberally with bread crumbs; then carefully break the eggs over this, and lay on them a few little pats of butter, and a seasoning of salt and pepper, and bake for about four minutes in a hot oven. OMELET WITH CHEESE. Break four egg's into a basin; then add two ounces of grated cheese, some pepper, and a little salt; beat the whole well:together, and fry in butter. SUGAR COOKIES. Stir half-a-pound of butter, and three-quarters of a pound of powdered sugar to a cream; then add four eggs, and beat them well in ; then add one gill of milk and a dessert- spoonful of Vanilla Extract ; then mix two teaspoonfuls of cream of Tartar, with flour sufficient to make a light dough, Knead quickly, and roll out rather thin. Cut into small. round cakes, dust them with sugar, and bake in a quick oven.

APPETISING DAINTY DISHES MADE WITH EGGS. EGG BISCUIT. Rub half-a-pound of butter, or leaf lard, into four pounds of flour, and make a dough of these with ten eggs and ten ounces of white auger. Roll out the dough into a sheet about an inch thick, priok the sheet all over, and cut the ' biscuit with a small cutter. Have a pot of boiling water and a pot of oold water. Drop the biscuits into the boiling water, and whea they rise to the top take them out, and put them into the cold water until they are cold; thee lay them en tins and bake them in a moderate oven. WINE BISCUIT. Take one pouad of sifted flour, ene egg, two tablespoon- fulls of powdered cigar, mix these with sufficient water to form a stiff dough, roll out thin, out into biscuit, and cake on buttered tins. • PLAIN OMELET. One egg, well-beaten, one teaspoonful of water, pepper and salt, fry in butter. BUTTERED EGGS. Bring about two ounces of butter to nearly boiling point, then add three or four well-beaten eggs. Keep stirring the k butter and eggs one way until they are hot without boiling and serve on hot buttered toast. If the mixture is allowed to boil it will curdle. • FRIED EGG SANDWICHES. Beat some eggs well, season with pepper and salt, fry them in butter as a pancake, when cold cut them in small square pieces and lay them between bread and butter.

PRINCESS ALICE PUDDING. Dissolve together 3ar. of sugar and 3se. of butter. Then take two good tablespoonsful of flour; and with three eggs, well beaten, mix into a smooth paste and gradually add one gill of milk, stirring all the time. And now add the dis- solved sugar and butter. Mix all well together and bake in saucers, well battered, for about twenty minutes. Before sending to table, a little preserve or marmalade may be put in centre, and one half of pudding placed over it. Enough for six saucers. LEMON PUDDING. 3 eggs, 1 teacup of sugar, 1 spoonful of butter, the juice and grated rind of two lemons, and a little salt. Beat all well together, and, lastly, add gradually one pint of milk. Bake half-an-hour in a moderate oven. LEMON CHEESECAKES. One pound loaf sugar, six ounces batter, four eggs well beaten; two lemons, both rind and juice. Keep stirring the mixture, over the fire, until the sugar is dissolved and it be- gins to thicken. It may also be done in a jar put into the oven, but care must be taken to keep stirring it. Line some patty-pans with puff-paste, put in the mixture, and bake for twenty minutes. YORKSHIRE BATTER PUDDING. Six ounces of flour, 1 pint of milk, 3 eggs, half a tea- spoonful of baking powder, and 1 teaspoonful of salt. Rub the baking powder quite smooth, mix it well in the flour, add the salt, and as much of the milk as will make it a stiff batter. beat it till smooth, then add the remainder of the milk, and the eggs well beaten. Melt some butter in a large flat dish or tin, pour in the batter, bake in a quick oven, and when baked cut it in squares.

ottrg. AT THE BEECHENrKEE. "Oh meet me by the stile," he wrote, "The stile beside the beechen tree." She was the pride o' the country-side; He was a sailor home from:sea. Beside the brook she wends her way, The birds sing high! the birds sing low! "Now will he come, or will he stay ?" Her heart says "Yes ;" her heart says "No." "I did not send an answer back, But he should know I love him well, For had I told him all he ask'd, I should have nothing more to tell." So through the wood she wends her way, The birds sing high! the birds sing low! "Now will he come, or will he stay ?" Her heart says "Yes ;" her heart says "No." She nears the spot—lie is not there,— " 0 faithless heart !" she faintly cries. But he is only hiding near, And soon he looks into her eyes. Beside the stile he holds her fast, The birds sings low, as if to bless. "Now give the answer, love,:at last." Her heart leaps high; her lips say "Yes." —Tv. Wilsey _Martin.
